I have a question to
direct to the Postmaster General with reference to the post office in the House of Commons, although perhaps the matter does not come directly under his control. The hon. gentleman must have received within the last few days complaints from some hon. members that obscene literature is being distributed in the boxes of the members, and that without any stamp and without any frank. speechtext: On the motion of Mr. Borden for Committee of Supply:

I wish again to call the attention of the Prime Minister and of the Minister of Railways to the grievance of which I complained on Friday last. From the remarks of the Minister of Railways I would gather that he is not quite familiar with the increased rates and the local conditions on the Prince Edward Island railway. Of course I am not surprised at that. When I mentioned that the rate of freight

on cordwood for a short distance was $7 a car, he seemed to think it was not very large. The fact is that the capacity of the cars on the Prince Edward Island railway is only about half as great as the capacity of the cars on the Intercolonial railway. Taking that fact into consideration the hon. minister will see that the charges on the main line of the Intercolonial would be about $12 to $14 per car. The rate in my province is prohibitive and is not in the interest of the railway. There are similar rates on lumber of all kinds. From the letter which I read on Friday last, it will be seen that the rates on many other articles are prohibitive.
I have been informed by gentlemen supporting the Government that apparently it is of little use bringing matters of this kind to the notice of the management at Moncton; that they do not seem to take seriously suggestions from business men. So far as the management in Prince Edward Island is concerned, it does not seem to have any power at all.
The Prime Minister will remember that before the last election, in the discharge -of his duty as leader of the Opposition, he came to our province and sympathized with the people there with reference to the very great difficulties they had in matters of .transportation. He certainly made statements to the effect that if he came into power he would have some remedy applied, and no one understood him to say that if he *came into power the rates would be increased. I am sure that the Prime Minister appreciates tne responsibility of any statement that he might have made under such circumstances ancL that he would not wish to mislead the people. This matter is more serious than the Minister of Railways or the Prime Minister appears to think. I am surprised that the members for Prince Edward Island supporting the Government are not pressing this matter more strenuously.
Most of the articles transported over the Prince Edward Island railway are not handled by the railway officials at all; they are loaded and unloaded by the people. Mixed freight and passenger trains run anyhow, whether freight is offered or not, and it would be very little extra expense to the railway to haul these cars which are loaded and unloaded by others. If the railway is to be of any service to the people, this matter should receive some *consideration from the Government. It may seem a small matter among the many (subjects that come before the Prime Minis-

ter, but I would again ask him at least to look into it.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I think the hon. gentleman is trying to mislead the people when he makes the statement that the cars on the Prince Edward Island railway do not carry over half what the cars on the main line do. This, I say, is not true, more than that, the hon. gentleman has never told the House and the country that we have cut out the third rate for the ferry across. This has never been done before, and is more in the interest of the people of Prince Edward Island than anything else we can do, until we get the ferry established. He has brought forward only one instance in which he says there is a hardship. In my opinion, he has not made out his case, because I know that the cars on the Prince Edward Island railway carry more than half what the cars on the main line do. If he has any other instances to give, I shall be glad to instruct the management to look into them.

Will the minister tell me the capacity of the cars on the Prince Edward (Island railway and the capacity of the cars on the Intercolonial railway? Then wre shall know whether my statement is true or not.

Perhaps I might be pardoned for asking permission to correct a statement I made last night in regard to the transportation of fish from the Maritime provinces to Montreal. I am reported in the unrevised ' Hansard ' as having said:
Now, a car is sent forward every day attached to an express train.
And further down I am reported to have
said:
We have provided for this car attached to an express train every day.
Apparently I must have made the statement, because I am reported in this way and my friends say that they so understood me. If I did make that statement, I did not intend to make it, and it was not correct. The statement I meant to make was that a cold storage express car was sent forward every Saturday. It is clear that this is the statement I intended to make from a subsequent passage in the report of my speech, in which I said:
A further arrangement was entered into last year with the express companies and the Intercolonial whereby a cold storage express car for the transportation of fish leaves Mulgrave for Montreal on Saturday of each week. Shipments from Halifax are taken on at Truro.
That was the statement I intended to make, but apparently, through inadvertence, I did not make that statement. I am not complaining of an incorrect report, as my friends say I did say what I am reported to have said, but I intended to say Saturday. At the time I was speaking from a report of the Superintendent of Fisheries in which the word Saturday was used. I desire to correct the mis-statement at the earliest opportunity.
We are to understand, then, that there is really no change in the arrangement for the transportation of fish?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The change is that an arrangement was made for an express car having cold storage facilities attached to an express train to leave Mulgrave every Saturday night so that the fish would arrive in Toronto every Monday morning.
On every express train that leaves Halifax on Saturday night?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It leaves Mulgrave every Saturday night.
There seems to be a misunderstanding about it among the fishing people.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The arrangement is described in this memorandum:
The uepartment felt that as it had shown the railways and express companies that the business can be made a big one, they should do their part in ottering further facilities. It, consequently, took up with the express companies and the Intercolonial railway, the question of placing refrigerator express cars at the disposal of the shippers. After much negotiation an agreement was entered into with the express companies and the railway, whereby a cold storage express car is placed at the disposal of the shippers from Mulgrave and Halifax one day each week. The car leaves Mulgrave on Saturdays, and at Truro, shipments from Halifax and other points along the Halifax and Southwestern railway are placed in it. It then proceeds to Montreal by the Maritime Express. The companies agreed to accept as a minimum carload for this car ten thousand pounds, instead of twenty thousand pounds. The department guarantees that the earnings will be at least those ten thousand pounds. Only on a few occasions since it was inaugurated in August last, have the shipments been below the minimum.
This car reaches Montreal Sunday night in time to connect with the Grand Trunk for Toronto, so that shipments can be removed from it and sent in ordinary express cars to Toronto which will reach the latter point Monday morning. Negotiations are being continued and it is anticipated that during the coming summer the arrangement will be extended so as to run through cold storage express ears from the Atlantic coast to Toronto, as well as to Montreal.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: She could not be stationed there all winter as she has other work to do. She was sent there, as was done in previous seasons, and the report received at the department this morning was that the Stanley had done the work she was sent to do and that the harbour is now open. As far as possible we keep the harbour open because we realize the great advantage of doing so in the case of a harbour doing such a large business as Sydney does.

I would point out to the minister that while it is very well to have a steamer go there and open the harbour still, unless she is in the immediate vicinity of the harbour all the time, the work done may not be of much value because the harbour might freeze up again and unless the boat is very near she could not re-open it.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We do the best we can. The steamer's headquarters are at Halifax. They were at one time at St. John, but an arrangement was made having regard to this ice breaking to have her at Halifax so that she would be nearer the ports.

Both Mr. McKenzie and myself have in our humble way been in-insisting upon the department having a permanent boat there. This is a harbour in which an immense business is carried on, and we would like to have an icebreaker there all the time during the winter season. The Stanley is not required in Halifax harbour as an icebreaker in the winter time, and I hope my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) will correct me if I am wrong in that, but I think I am right. Why should not the Stanley be stationed at Louisburg which is open the year around and then she would be in a position to get into Sydney harbour whenever required. It is incumbent upon the department to give us an icebreaker in that part of the country.

I would like to call the attention of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to the custom that has prevailed in his department, and under the late Government, of having the headquarters of the steamers at St. John, N.B. That has always seemed to me a very great mistake. I think some of the steamers should have their headquarters at Yarmouth or on the bay of Fundy. In the case of the recent wreck of the Cobequid, had one of the Government steamers been stationed at Yarmouth instead of at St. John, there is no doubt that the people could have been rescued without having to wait 36 hours. I cannot see that the expense would be heavier at Yarmouth than at St. John, I am sure there are many occasions during the winter time when a ship at Yarmouth would be very useful. Buoys are continually going adrift on the coast of Nova Scotia and it would be very convenient to have a boat there to locate them. I think it would be in the interests of the department and of the public to have one of those boats stationed at Yarmouth and the other stationed at St. John and I would recommend the minister to take this into consideration.

Will the minister say whether he will take it into conside ation?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I did not know that
my hon. friend expected an answer. Any suggestion made in good faith will of course be considered. I may say the reason why these steamers have been kept at St. John and Halifax is that one agency is at Halifax and the other at St. John and the steamers are naturally kept as far as possible at the points where the agencies are. But I may say to my hon. friend, that if there had been a steamer at Yarmouth I do not think the people on the Cobequid would have been rescued any earlier. I think some statement to that effect is made in the report of the Wreck Commissioner, filed yesterday afternoon. He stated that in view of the heavy seas running it is doubtful whether the people could have been taken off at an earlier time, even if the rescue boats had been there. They had to wait till the waves calmed down before they could proceed with the rescue work.

If one of the Government
boats had been able to lay by the Cobequid all night, it would certainly have been a great relief to the passengers knowing that some vessel was at hand. I still think it reasonable to ask that one of these steamers stationed at St. John or Halifax should be kept at Yarmouth.
There are many times, I know myself, when buoys go adrift, and word has to be sent to St. John and this boat brought away down to Yarmouth or down in the bay of Fundy before these buoys can be rescued, whereas if a steamer were lying at Yarmouth, if buoys got adrift or a vessel were wrecked, it would be right on the spot. This is a question that should receive the due consideration of the minister.

rivets in Collingwood?
