speechtext: 1 did not examine the rivets. I think that the contract was let before the change of government took place.

So much the better.
Mr.A.K. MACLEAN: Would the minister please inform us as to the repairs for which tenders are asked and for which tenders are not asked? How is it settled-according to the amount of the repairs to be made?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It depends upon the nature of the repairs. When a vessel is new it is an easier matter for the officials of the department, like Mr. Ferguson and other technical officers who have charge of this work, to prepare a specification on which tenders can be asked, but when a vessel is old and a lot of work has to be removed and torn down and it is impossible to tell what has to be done until you commence tearing down, it is very frequently thought that it is not desirable to ask for tenders because it is impossible for any one to know before hand what the work will amount to.

That is hardly an answer to the question I asked. Surely the department must have some rule about this. Certainly the proper rule would be that the department should ask for tenders, perhaps not in all cases, but in the majority of cases and the cases in which it was not done should not reach any substantial figure.
If a boat were to be repaired in Halifax at a cost of $500, what course would be pursued? Whether the boat was old or new should not make any difference. Are tenders asked publicly, or are they quietly solicited from friends of the Government and those whose names are on the patronage list?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Is there a
patronage list now?
In Halifax there is not only a patronage list but a patronage committee.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Surely not.

The Prime Minister, who represents that constituency, apparently does not undertake to discharge the duties which ordinarily devolve upon a supporter of the Government in respect to patronage, and so they have a patronage committee. In Halifax the policy which would guide the department would be largely determined by that committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The manner of doing the repairs would largely depend upon the report of Mr. Ferguson, inspector of Government steamers, and Mr. McConkey, inspector of repairs to Government vessels. These gentlemen would be guided by the condition of the vessel and the nature of work to be done as to whether they would recommend day's work or contract. The great bulk of these tenders are asked, not by public advertisement in the newspapers, but by asking certain persons and firms, whose names are upon a list for that purpose.
In 1910 the Nova Scotia Iron Works of Dartmouth were paid apparently $5,363 under contract. Were tenders invited in that case before the contract was made?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I will have to look that up.

What is the
meaning of the charges set out in the Auditor General's Report by the Naval Service Department against the Marine Department?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I suppose that is work
done for the Marine Department in the dockyards at Halifax and Nanaimo, which are under the control of the Naval Service Department.

I understand that the
cutters of the Customs Department are under the joint supervision of the Department of Marine and the Department of Customs.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The Marine Department
has no control over the Customs cutters.
The practice used to be to have joint control.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: The Marine Department supplies the officers and crews and pays them, and that amount is refunded by the Department of Customs, but the steamers are absolutely under the control of the Department of Customs.

That is exactly as I
understood it. I wish to ask the minister if in October or November last a yacht was purchased for the use of the Customs Department, and which yacht now is said to be in winter quarters at Prescott. From whom was the yacht purchased, for what purpose, and what price was paid?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: The only yacht I have any knowledge of is a yacht seized by the Department of Customs at Prescott some time last spring, I think. It was hauled up at Prescott and repaired and the owners abandoned it.
Who was the owner of the yacht?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: We could not find the owner. I think he left the country a year or two ago. Two men in Brockville, the captain and the engineer, had claims against the yacht. Their claims were paid by the Department of Customs, and the yacht, after being refitted, was sent on to St. John, N.B.

My hon. friend can find all the details in the Register, because every boat is registered. This yacht was towed from Montreal up the river as far as Prescott or Kingston about the end of October or the beginning of November last, and quartered there for the winter. Names have been given to me, which I do not care to produce, but I should like to know from the hon. minister if it is not true that his department purchased such a yacht.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
We have no record in the Customs Department of the purchase of
such a yacht. The yacht I refer to was purchased in the month of July and was sent down to St. John.

Did the department
purchase any yacht as late as October or November last?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: Not that I know of.

Will the hon. minister find out if within the last five months any yacht has been purchased by the Department of Customs and quartered for the winter either at Prescott or at Kingston, and give his answer this evening?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
I will give the hon.
member an answer within half an hour.

I saw in the papers
lately that the Department of Marine and Fisheries had given a contract for the building of a vessel to Vickers Sons and Maxim, of Montreal, and that the construction of the vessel had been commenced in Montreal. What truth is there in that statement?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
There is no truth in it.
No contract has been awarded. Tenders have been asked for and are coming in for the construction of a dredge and also for the construction of an ice-breaker. The time for receiving these tenders is not up yet.

If tenders are received from Great Britain and from Canada, will the hon. minister give the preference to Canadian builders or to British builders, and is there any condition as to where the vessels are to be constructed?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
We are asking for tenders
for a vessel to be constructed m Canada.
Then the statement that the vessel has to be built in Canada is true?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That statement is true.

Of course it is not
known where in Canada the vessel will be built?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No.
When were the tenders to be in?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I think they were to be
in on the 31st day of January. We had a communication from certain builders stating that they desired to tender, but could not get in their tenders in time. They asked us to extend the time for receiving

tenders, and we extended it until the 5th day of this month.

What is the estimated
cost of the ice-breaker?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Half a million dollars for an ice-breaker of the most modern construction for the St. Lawrence river.
I have seen in the press that the two ice-breakers, the Montcalm and the Lady Grey, have been removed from Quebec to the Maritime provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No. They are at work on the St. Lawrence, and their special business is to keep the ice broken on the St. Lawrence river. This has two results: it avoids floods in the spring of the year, and it causes the river to open much sooner, so that navigation will open earlier.

When I saw that statement in the press, I wondered whether my hon. friend had listened to the complaints of eertain people from Quebec in regard to ice floes blocking the harbour of Quebec during the wiater. I do not think they have any serious ground for complaint, and, as my hon. friend states, the work performed by the two steamers is most valuable, not only to navigation proper, but to prevent a repetition of the devastating floods from which we suffered some years ago. I am glad that the hon. gentleman will not listen to any such complaints.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We listened to them, but we were not convinced by the representations that were made.

In the list of steamers
which my hon. friend read a little earlier in the afternoon, how many of the vessels are ice-breakers? Where do they operate? Do they operate in the same place each season?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The Champlain is an icebreaker and is used in the ferry running from Riviere Ouelle to Murray bay. The Earl Grey i3 an ice-breaker in the Prince Edward Island service. The Lady Grey is an ice-breaker, used on the St. Lawrence river and on the ship channel during the summer. The Minto is an ice-breaker in the Prince Edward Island service. The Montcalm is an ice-breaker, used on the St. Lawrence river and in the lighthouse and buoy service in Quebec during the summer months. The Stanley is an ice-breaker, used in the light-house and buoy service in Nova Scotia, in breaking ice in different

harbours where it is possible to do so, and also in making trips across to the Magdalen islands.

Are they kept on the
same routes each season?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
Does the Stanley make occasional trips to the Magdalen islands during the winter for mail purposes?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The Stanley has made one trip to the Magdalen islands. We hope - she will be able to make others.

I have received a letter from the Rev. Father Turbide, one of the most prominent clergymen on the islands, who states that the service is badly needed. He informs me that there is a lack of coal on the islands this winter. I do not know for what reason, but the islanders were deprived of their usual supply of coal last fall. I shall be pleased to know that my hon. friend will see that the Stanley makes one or two additional trips before the month of March. Does my hon. friend know if the service between Riviere Ouelle on the south shore and Murray bay on the north shore has been interrupted, and the cause of the interruption of the trips made by the Champlain?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I understand that the service this year from Riviere Ouelle to Murray bay has not been satisfactory. A new wharf is in course of construction at Murray bay, and at present proper protection is not afforded to steamers at that place. We have had a great deal of correspondence about it, and have done the best we could. Circumstances which were not under the control of our department have made it almost impossible for us to give a3 satisfactory a service as should be given.

If the service is not re-established this winter, there will be very great hardship, because that is the only line of communication for the whole of the north shore with Quebec and Montreal. It is true that a new and very much needed wharf is being built at Murray bay. If my honourable friend will look into the matter he will find that although the landing facilities at Murray bay are not as good as they should be, better facilities may be be obtained elsewhere, for instance at Cap a l'Aigle, Les Eboulements, St. Irenee or Baie St. Paul. Any of these places are a little out of the way, but the people on

the north shore would have at least communication with the south shore and with Quebec and Montreal if landings were established at any of these points. I would ask my hon. friend to look into this matter and see that the people are given proper communication, as they are now as much isolated as the people of the Magdalen Islands.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Efforts are now being made to effect arrangements by which the Lady Grey, when she can be spared, will be put on the route from Quebec to Murray bay. At present the trouble is that she cannot remain at Murray bay for any length of time, but efforts are being made to give a more satisfactory service than at present exists.

I read in the papers last night that the steamer Montcalm was leaving in the morning on a cruise to the gulf, the vicinity of the Seven islands and the north shore. On a previous occasion I read that it was the intention of the department to keep these steamers this winter on the St. Lawrence, with a view to keeping the river open up to Three Rivers or lake St. Peter. Representing the county of Champlain, you are familiar, Mr. Chairman, with the conditions in that district, but perhaps you have not suffered as much from the results of ice jams on the St. Lawrence river below Three Rivers as we have further up. When the ice jams in this part of the river the counties of St. Maurice, Champlain and Maskinonge are flooded and a great deal of damage is done. In the years 1906, 1907, 1908 and 1909 the Montcalm and the Lady Grey came regularly to this part of the river and kept the channel open, and in the spring there were no floods and no damage was done. On one occasion the Montcalm ran short of coal at Three Rivers and was caught in the ice, and, no tugs or ot-ier boats being available, she eouiu not work her way out and had to winter at Three Rivers. The consequence was that the boat could not do any work at Cap a la Roche, the ice jammed, and there was a flood on both sides of the St. Lawrence. Barns and houses were torn down, wharfs were broken away, and considerable damage was done on the shores of the river. If it be the intention of the Government to charter boats as ice-breakers and keep them at that work, 1 do not see any necessity of their breaking ice except where the ice takes, for that is where there is liable to be great damage to property. If it is not the intention of the department to recall the Montca'm and have her perform the services for which she was intended, I would urge the Government to take such steps as will give a measure of protection to the people along the shores of the St. Lawrence river between Cap a la Roche and lake St. Peter.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: As far as the breaking of ice in the St. Lawrence is concerned, these boats are under the direction of Mr. For-neret, who is in charge of the dredging operations on the river St. Lawrence. What my hon. friend has said about the desirability of keeping the ice broken so as to prevent these floods is absolutely correct. When certain conditions of tide and weather prevail, the boats are not required for the purpose of breaking ice, and under such circumstances it has been customary to send the boats to the Seven Islands and other places with which there is no communication, in order that the people in those districts may be able to get supplies and have communication with the outside world. That policy has been pursued for the last ten years and, I understand, satisfactorily so. The boats are there for the purpose of breaking ice in the ship channel during the winter season, and no good purpose would be served in keeping them there when they are not necessary for the purpose of breaking ice. Under such circumstances it is much better to have them render service to the people of Seven Islands and other points. They only go under such conditions as I have referred to, and when, in the opinion of the superintendent of the St. Lawrence channel, they can do so without in any way impairing their efficiency as ice-breakers.

I have every confidence in Mr. Forneret; against him I have nothing whatever to say. I would call attention to the fact that the ice has taken-I have crossed the river on the ice between the counties of Champlain and Nicolet. The year the boat was caught in the ice at Three Rivers-1912; they called it the Borden flood, I think- much damage was done, and if these boats are sent down the river this year, and the work is not started at once, I am satisfiied that the result will be the same. Is it the policy of the Government to try to keep the channel open during the winter, as was stated in the Conservative press last fall?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It is, certainly-to keep the ice broken so that there shall be no floods, and so that navigation will be open early in the spring.
I may tell the minister that the ice has frozen over the river and is thickening all the time, just at the places where the boat ought to be to-day.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I shall certainly call the attention of Mr. Forneret to what my hon. friend says. As evidence of the fact that we are desirous of doing all that is possible in the matter, I may say that we have asked for tenders for a foreign ice-breaker to be used on the St. Lawrence river as an icebreaker, and for no other purpose. It has been found that the practice of having boats constructed to be used not only as icebreakers, but for other purposes during the summer, is one which has not been very much in the public interest. These boats built as ice-breakers are tremendous consumers of coal, and their operation for ordinary purposes during the summer is very expensive. The new boat is being constructed for use as an ice-breaker only. It will be of the most modern construction, and I am told by the naval architect of the department that it will be equal to any ice-breaker in any part of the world. When that boat is ready and in operation I do not think that there will be any further complaints. Because of the fact that the people living at Seven Islands are entirely without means of communication with outside districts, a tremendous pressure is brought to bear on the department-and the same is true of the Magdalen Islands-to have boats sent there from time to time to make conditions of living a little more pleasant than they are when the people are absolutely shut out from the outside world. But if by doing so we are imperilling the work upon the St. Lawrence, then the very greatest care ought to be exercised.
I do not want to be understood as trying to discriminate against the people of the Seven islands or any other place, but they have the Druid that I know of and the Montmagny.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: They are not ice-breakers, they cannot do that service in winter.

These boats could go
down to the Seven islands, they are strong boats and go down there in the spring and late fall.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: They are not built for that purpose, they could not do it in the winter season.

At page N-22 of the Auditor General's Report, there is an account for $5,353 paid to the Nova Scotia 
Iron Works at Dartmouth. Were tenders asked for that work?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The purchasing agent tells me that those repairs were done by tender.

On page N-22 there is a payment to Stewart, Bruce & Co., Charlottetown, of nearly $3,000 for repairs to the steamer Montcalm. There was also a sum of over $4,500 paid to the same firm for repairs to the Earl Grey. These two accounts are made up of small amounts, but in the aggregate the amount is quite substantial for the year. Was this done after tenders?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The purchasing agent tells me that the first item is made up of different small items. It was not done by tender. Practically this is the only firm in Charlottetown with a shop of the kind necessary to do the work of that character and this is the firm who for many years past, no matter what Government has been in power, have been doing work for the Department of Marine and Fisheries.
Is this the only firm in Charlottetown capable of doing this class of work?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
That is what I am told
by the purchasing agent of the department.
When supplies of the value of over $100 are purchased what is the practice of the department? Are tenders solicited from friends of the Government or from the public?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: In many cases tenders are asked from friends of the Government. Thexe are cases when they are asked from people on both sides of politics, when people who are not friends of the Government are asked to submit figures.
What amount determines the policy of the Government as to whether friends of the Government or the public are asked to submit tenders?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The purchasing agent tells me that the same policy prevails as has prevailed for many years past. The local agent of the department asks for figures and the people who are leaders in different lines of commerce supply the different lines of goods wanted. Figures are submitted and the lowest prices are accepted and all goods are obtained on a competitive basis.

But sometimes
the competition is confined to well known friends of the Government.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I think that would be correct.

Regardless of the
amount purchased during a season.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I think that where the
amounts are very large, tor large quantities of iron, &c., tenders are asked.
What course does the minister direct to be taken by purchasing agents in St. John, for instance.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: In St. John four or five different firms are asked to figure.
Friends of the Government?	,

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I think they are in all
cases friends of the Government.
Then surely there will come a time when the amount would be so large that the hon. gentlemen would be mindful of the public interest and not so regardful of his own party friends.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I think you have competition enough amongst them to bring them down to the lowest price.
What is the amount?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: There is no hard and fast rule.
In St. John must the agent inquire of the minister what he shall do?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Before the agent enters
into any contract he submits figures to the purchasing agent of the department in x Ottawa, who has been in that position for a number of years; the purchasing agent of the department examines the figures and satisfies himself that the amounts charged are only fair and reasonable charges tor the work to be done.
Does he consult the member for the city and county of St. John?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Not at all; in matters of that sort he practically consults no one. He has large responsibilities on his shoulders as purchasing agent.
Is there a patronage list for St. John in the Marine Department?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No.
For Halifax ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No.	*
Where is this list kept ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The purchasing agent tells me that he has no patronage list but has a knowledge in every community in Canada of people engaged in different lines of business and he is guided by that.

I do not think this was the practice under the late Government.
If it was, it never had the concurrence of
lion, gentleman opposite.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The purchasing agent tells me the practice is exactly the same as that which prevailed under my predecessors in office.
The Minister of Marine did not approve of this practice.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I was not in the House.

The hon. gentleman was out of the House, but he took very good care to let the public in New Brunswick know that he did not approve of this departmental practice. I remember the hon. ' gentleman making a speech in the election of 1911 in St. John in which he condemned this practice in the most severe fashion.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I think my hon. friend is entirely mistaken; I do not think I ever made a speech in my life in which I condemned the system of purchase being carried on in the Department of Marine and Fisheries. It may be that I should have done so, but I did not.
The minister spoke against reciprocity.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: On many occasions.
There is a practice in the Railways and Canals Department, and I think in the Public Works Department, that all amounts over $5,000 must be advertised.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Anything over $5,000 in our department is purchased by tender, and on many occasions for less amounts.
Open to the public ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.

I would like to ask about a number of items, found at page No. 13 of the Auditor General's Report, amounting to $20,431.50 paid to George T. Davie & Son, of Levis, tor repairs to some steamer. I do not think it is stated in the item what steamer it is. I would like to know if tenders were asked for in this case, and in the other cases where this firm has made repairs to steamers at Levis; and if so, wihether these tenders

were open to the public or were the contracts awarded simply by private letters written to the firm.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I cannot give my hon. friend exact information, as the payment he refers to occurred before I was minister. I believe the circumstances were something like this: The Earl Grey was taking the Governor General down the river and ran ashore. She was very badly damaged, and was repaired by the Davie firm, who were the lessees of the Government dry dock at Quebec. There was no other place where the Earl Grey could have been repaired. Of course I am speaking of something for which I have no responsibility at all. But I am told an estimate was made of the cost of repairs by the inspector, Mr. Ferguson, and, based on that, the minister of that day entered into a contract with the Davie firm.	-

There is another item in which the name of the Davie firm appears. On page N-10 it says:
Geo. T. Davie & Son, Levis, replacing propeller blade, &c., ?3,094.
That is in connection with the steamer Champlain. Were tenders asked for, and if so, in what manner?	*

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am informed that the Davie firm is the only company in the city of Quebec that is able to make repairs to a ship beneath its water line. It is the only firm in Quebec that has the facilities and the docking appliances for doing that, and therefore any vessel requiring such work has to go to the Davie firm. The custom is to have a careful report and estimate made by the technical officers of the department, and upon that report a contract is entered into.

My hon. friend can sleep on both ears every evening so long as he has as honest and straightforward a purchasing agent as the one now in the employ of his department. I can testify to his ability and to his honesty. But at the same time I am surprised at the offhand way in which my hon. friend speaks of the system whereby tenders are given to a select few-a select few Tories of course. My hon. friend was not in the House prior to 1911. Of course he had some experience of the House in 1891, but several hon. gentlemen who were sitting on this side of the House prior to 1911, simply roasted to death my predecessor in office, Hon. L. P. Bro-

deur, because, forsooth, he followed the practice which has been accepted and gladly followed by the present Minister of Marine and Fisheries. This is the best possible vindication of the policy of the Hon. Mr. Brodeur. Day in and day out he was taunted by the Conservative Opposition because he accepted tenders from Grit firms, at very reasonable prices, for repairs to some steamers.
He was being roasted about his trip to England.

My hon. friend could take a trip to England and learn many things there, but this is not a case of trips to England or trip3 to Zululand. The question is whether my hon. friend who now interrupts me did not attack Mr. Brodeur, the predecessor of the present incumbent, because he awarded contracts to a few Grit tenderers at a very reasonable price when he was in office? To-day the present Minister of Marine and Fisheries furnishes us with the most complete vindication of Mr. Brodeur. He says:	I
followed the system of my predecessor. That is about all we can expect from a Tory Government. Each time this Government is taken to task they reproach us with having done a similar thing while we were in office. They admit now that what we did then was honest and fair, but at that time they criticised it. Hon. gentlemen were simply making political capital in order to prejudice the mind of the electors. I am glad to see the minister following the policy adopted by his predecessor, Mr. Brodeur, and taking the advice of this much abused yet able and active purchasing agent appointed by the Laurier Government, Mr. Doutre.
Do I understand that all purchases made by the department must first receive the approval of the purchasing agent?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes, for every dollar.
Would that apply to repairs on a ship as well?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes, to everything.
Then before repairs are commenced on a ship the rates pertaining to the different items have to be approved by the purchasing agent. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
No work is undertaken in the way of repairs to ships or anything of that sort, until the purchasing agent has issued a warrant for such work and no

money ia paid until he examines the bills and has certified that the charges are correct.

Does not the minister
think he should lay down a rule for the guidance of his officer, as (to when he should ask for public tenders, and when the contract should be given to friends of the Government?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
In cases where there is no question about asking for public tenders, the purchasing agent would go to the deputy head or to myself and discuss the matter.
I want to say to my hon. friend that it has not been my practice to interfere with the judgment of the purchasing agent in matters of that sort.

How does the purchasing agent know who are the friends of me
Government?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I suppose the purchasing
agent, being a man of affairs, has a pretty fair knowledge of that.
Take the case of a government ship buying supplies from a merchant on the coast of my constituency. Who advises them where to buy their supplies?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not know what goods are purchased in the constituency of my hon. friend except goods purchased by the steward. The stewards are free agents and can purchase where they see fit.
That is for provisions?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes. I do not know what else they could purchase along the coast of Guysborough.
Supplies lor ships?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
That sort of thing would
be purchased, I should say, at the agencies through the agents of the department and not by the officers of the ships. They would have to go to the agents of the department except there might be an occasion when something would have to be purchased when there was not time to consult with the agent. But I cannot imagine that anything of importance would be purchased except through the agents of the department.
Coal?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Coal is supplied by contract, and of course coal is a thing that has a well established market price.
Where was the coal purchased last year in the county of Gasp6 for the Government steamers?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I understand that it was
purchased from a gentleman named Carter.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: Might I be permitted to give the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemiuex) an answer to the question he asked me a few minutes ago? The hon. member for Rouville asked if a yacht had been purchased by the Customs Department.
A yacht or a boat.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: I have a memorandum from the Assistant Commissioner of Customs in which he tells me that no yacht has been purchased by the Customs Department during the last six months and quartered for the winter at Prescott or Kingston. As far as I am personally concerned if a steamer had been purchased for the Customs Department and it had been at any place on the St. Lawrence west of Montreal I would have known something about it.
What about the yacht said to have been seized and quartered at Prescott?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: I say that a yacht was seized at Prescott or Brockville and that only the parties that had any claim against it were paid. It was hauled up immediately on the marine works and repaired and the Department of Customs paid the Department of Marine and Fisheries for the repairs. The boat was then towed to Kingston, brought down the Rideau canal to Ottawa and taken from Ottawa to St. John direct; it was not used in any way on the St. Lawrence river after it came off the ways at Prescott.
Will the hon. gentleman tell us who was the owner of the yacht and how it was registered?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: It was an American yacht.
The yacht was the property of some one; it would have been easy to find out.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: There was no way of finding it out.
Was it the Phantom?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: No, the name of the yacht was the Albatross. The boat 5 p.m. had been used on the St. Lawrence for a year before it was found out by the preventive staff that it was an American yacht.
How much was paid for the repairs and what was devoted to the people who had a claim against it?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
If I remember rightly the
master had a claim of about $150 and the engineer of $300 or $400. That was all that was paid by the Customs Department except the amount paid to the Marine Department for repairs. I could not exactly say what that was. It took considerable to repair her and to put her in the condition necessary to be used at St. John. She went directly from Prescott through the Rideau canal to St. John, N.B.; where, she is being employed in the service.
The minister has told us that coal is always purchased by tender.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Where coal is required in
large quantities, such as at the Sorel shipyards and at Quebec where a large number of steamers are supplied from, it is purchased by tender, but sometimes it is necessary to purchase it without tender, as in the case of the -comparatively small quantity purchased at Gasp6 from Mr. Carter.
What system is pursued when tenders are asked for ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We buy small quantities at the ordinary market price which would have to be approved by the purchasing agent.

How is that ordinary market price ascertained ?
Mr: HAZEN: I suppose it is well understood in any -community what the ordinary market price of a certain commodity would be at a certain time. Mr. Doutre, the purchasing agent, tells me that he has a list showing what the cost of coal should be for delivery at every point in Canada.

How is it, then, that a certain quantity of run-of-mine coal was purchased in Charlottetown at five dollars per ton, and a certain quantity of steamer coal, which is of better quality, was purchased at $5.75 per ton ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The purchasing agent informs me that the person who was supplying at $4.70 a ton ran out of coal, and we were forced to pay a higher price for a small quantity to get delivery at the time we wanted it. That seems to be a peculiar case.

For a department that uses so much coal, would it not be better

to make a contract direct with the coal companies, especially in the Maritime provinces ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That is what we do.
You do not contract for your coal supplies on the St. Lawrence ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes, we do. We enter into a contract direct with the coal company for coal used at Sorel, and Quebec, and St. John, and Halifax, and Montreal. I am informed that the Nova Scotia Steel Company has the large end of that contract.
What price does the department pay the coal company ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am informed that the prices are: $4.03 per ton delivered -at Sorel and Quebec; $4 per ton delivered at Montreal, bunkered; $3.75 at Halifax, and about $3.80 at St. John.
What do you pay at Gaspd ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: 48 tons were purchased at Gasp6 for $5 a ton from Mr. A. T. Carter, and 100 tons at $5.50.
Did the minister state that the stewards of the vessels had complete control of the purchase of supplies of stores on the departmental boats ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That is the fact.
Is there a patronage committee in Yarmouth ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: A what ?
A Tory patronage committee ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I have no knowledge of such a committee.

I can tell the minister that after the change of Government, the very first visit that the steward of the lightship Lurcher made to Yarmouth, he was met before he landed on the wharf by a member of the patronage committee in Yarmouth and told he had to buy his provisions from certain persons there. I have no objection whatever to those from whom he was asked to buy his provisions, but the result was that this gentleman made up his mind that he had to buy his stores- and having a contract with the Marine and Fisheries Department to supply the men at a certain price-he ought to have an opportunity to buy them at the cheapest place. The members of the patronage committee, not only having advised him but ordered him to buy from certain per-

sons, and as he found there was no money in continuing in the work, he resigned his position as steward, and a new man was put in his place.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: He was very foolish to resign his position, because nobody in Yarmouth or anywhere else had authority from the department to compel him to resign, or to prevent .him from buying provisions from any person he wanted to buy from. His contract from the department was to supply the men and officers at so much per head, and all he had to do was (to carry out that work in good faith.

Are the coal supplies
for the Marine Department, which are from the companies, bought under tender?
Mr. HAZEhi. Yes.
I ask the minister to make it plain that the stewards of these boats are at liberty to purchase stores from any person from whom they see nt to purchase, without losing their position.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That is absolutely correct. The department makes a contract with them and the business of the department is simply to see that their work is properly carried out.

I am very glad to hear the minister make that statement, because I think it is only fair, when these men take a contract for a certain price, that they should be permitted to buy their goods wherever they can buy them cheapest.
Will the department always protect a purchasing agent, we will say the purchasing agent at St. John, if he buys supplies from those from whom he can purchase for the lowest possible price?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
There is no purchasing
agent at St. John, but we will certainly protect the agent at St. John or anywhere else if he, first of all, submits the matter to the purchasing agent of the department at Ottawa, gets his warrant to proceed with the purchase, and if the purchasing agent at Ottawa afterwards certifies that the prices are proper prices.
And you would not take notice of any protest you might receive from say a defeated Conservative candidate, protesting against these purchases or asking for the removal from office of such a man?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: All I can say is that other things being equal any government would prefer to have purchases made from its friends rather than from those who are not. That is the principle and policy which every government, under our system of government, has acted upon since the world began. So far as purchasing is concerned, I have no doubt there is not a port-in Canada at which good goods cannot be purchased from persons of one political faith just as cheaply as from those of another political faith. Other things being equal, I would expect the purchases to be made from those who are friends of the Government, but I would not expect the agent to so purchase, if it were against the public interest to do so, or if he had to pay higher prices.
What does the minister do to protect a purchasing agent against a patronage committee?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The purchasing agent at Ottawa has a thorough knowledge of the value of goods, or he would not be fit to be purchasing agent. He knows the value of goods at St. John, or Halifax, or anywhere else, and he will not certify and allow the goods to be paid for unless the prices are right.
Then why permit the existence of a patronage committee?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
My hon. friend is too old a politician to ask a question of that sort. He knows that when his party were in power, and when other parties were in power also, people in different constituencies would organize themselves into patronage committees and make representations to the member from that constituency, or to the Government with regard to appointments to office, and as to from whom purchases should be made and so on. That is all very well, but after all, the responsibility for what is done must rest upon the responsible head of the department and the permanent officials, and they will take pains to guard the public interest. I think honourable gentlemen are indulging in a good deal of nonsense when they say that governments will not help their own friends. All governments will help their own friends if they can do so, and if by doing so they are doing nothing that is against the public interest. But governments have no right to purchase from their own friends in preference to their opponents, if by doing so they pay higher prices for the goods purchased. I think that is the

correct principle under our system of party government, and when we talk about governments not favouring their own friends when they can do so without injury to the public interest, we are talking what, at the bottom of our hearts, we know is not the principle which governs to-day anywhere.
Would the minister have any objection to show us the patronage list in his department?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Mr. Doutre says he has no patronage list.

I suppose that in some constituencies it is the practice, and possibly has been the practice, to have a patronage committee, but I have very little respect for the member representing a constituency who permits that, and will not take the responsibility himself.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: In the end, the representative of the constituency has to take the responsibility.

It is an anomaly in the political system obtaining in this country. I am not complaining so much of preference being shown to friends of the Government by ministers when purchasing, but the minister justifies that upon the ground that the public interest does not suffer. I say the public interest frequently does suffer, and we will be able to show some ministers of the Crown, before the session is over, that by reason of the patronage system public interests have suffered. If the minister adheres to the policy of purchasing from friends of the Government, he should lay down some rule for the guidance of his officers as to when this favour should be shown to friends of the Government; there should be some limit to it in the amount or the quantity of purchases. The minister has been asked several times this afternoon to establish some rule with reference to the matter, but he has failed to do so.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The universal instruction
that the purchasing agent gets is: that he is to purchase the goods used by the department to the best possible advantage from the standpoint of the department and from the standpoint of the public interest. I am satisfied that the purchasing agent of the department lives up to that rule. If the hon. gentleman can show me where, in our department, we have been paying excessive prices for any article, I will be very much surprised indeed. There might be a single case that would pass by

accident, but I believe that all the articles we are purchasing are purchased on fair and proper terms, and in many cases we are paying less than the prices paid by private individuals throughout the country for similar goods.

I had not the
Marine Department specially in mind when I made that observation; it was the principle I was referring to.
The purchasing agent in the Marine and Fisheries Department is a gentleman who has been in office for many years.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: For some years.

So far as I know that gentleman has always filled the position with very great care and satisfaction, and I do not see why he should make any mistake at the present time when he was able to do perfectly right in past years.
How are the men for the ice-breakers and other Government vessels selected?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
They are selected by the
agents of the department. I have no hesitation in saying that the agent of the department, at Charlottetown for instance, would consult with and take recommendations from members for the constituency supporting the Government, Mr. McLean and Mr. Nicholson. The agent would not take their recommendations unless he was satisfied of the competency of the men recommended. If the men are thoroughly competent, an agent is quite within his right in accepting the recommendations of the member for the constituency.

I thought the captains
were consulted with regard to the men.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The agent probably consults the captain.
Has the agent the privilege of refusing any man who he knows is not qualified?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
If the captain of one of
those vessels said that a man was not competent, he would not be forced upon the captain. It would not be in the interest of the public service to force a captain to take a man who was not competent.

During the campaign of 1911 one of the policies of the present Prime Minister, in order to obtain the support of the electorate in certain por-

tions of Canada, was the affording of medical aid and free medicine to fishermen.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
That could not properly
come up under this item, which is a marine item.

I thought you
might carry the doctor and the medicine around in these ships.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: This matter would properly come under the question of fisheries. I have no objection, however, to discussing the matter now.

I would like to
have it discussed now.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The matter is receiving a
great deal of consideration at the hands of the officers of the Department of Fisheries. They are endeavouring to form some satisfactory scheme for giving the suggested medical service to fishermen. They find it a very difficult problem to solve. Although many of them are men of experience, and have consulted men outside of the department, members of the House and others who are interested in the matter, they have found it most difficult to form any scheme that will be satisfactory and that will be within reasonable financial bounds. Although the problem is such a difficult one, we have not altogether despaired of solving it. My first knowledge of the matter came after the election, when I became a member of the House and a member of the Government.
Is it intended to supply all the fishermen in Canada with free medical attendance and free medicine, and their families as well?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Nothing will be gained by discussing the details of a matter that is at present under consideration and that has not been fully worked out.
What officials are discussing the matter?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The Deputy Minister of
Marine and Fisheries, the Superintendent of Fisheries and others.

In regard to the construction of ships in Canada, has my hon. friend laid it down as a policy that in future vessels of the description of those used by the Department of Marine and Fisheries will be built in Canada? I would like my hon. friend to state that positively, because the draft and tonnage of these ships would certainly entitle the Canadian 27
ship-builders to have the first consideration. There should be no hesitation in giving our Canadian ship-builders the preference, not only of tendering but of getting the contract.
Mr- HAZEN: Since I have been in the department, not a dollar of our money has gone outside Canada for the building of ships. When I entered the department, certain vessels for British Columbia waters and the Halifax lightship were under con* struction. These were completed. My policy is this, that in the case of all vessels that will be required for the Marine and Fisheries Department in future, it is my intention, with the approval of the Council, to ask for tenders for these vessels to be built in Canada.
The Canadian shipbuilder has no protection in regard to vessels of this class. There is no duty upon ships of British register; they come into Canada complete in every respect, with their napkins, their china and all their appointments. The rate of wages is lower in Great Britain than it is here, and the result is that the Canadian shipbuilder is at a very great disadvantage in competing for vessels required for the Government service.
Two dredges are now being built at Col-lingwood for use on the (St. (Lawrence river; they will be in commission next year. They have been built since I came into office. In the tenders for the icebreaker to which I referred, the condition is that it must be built in Canada. It seems to me that we cannot protect the shipbuilding industry in the way in which we can protect other industries. The only way protection could be given to the shipbuilding industry would be by giving a bounty of so much a ton upon ships built in Canada. Whether that would be acceptable to the country or not, I am not prepared to state at present.

I must congratulate
the hon. gentleman on his policy. It should appeal to every good Canadian. The Government of Canada has already bonused quite heavily some of the shipbuilding firms, and it would be a pity if, for the construction of ships which can evidently be built in 'Canada, the preference were given to outside firms. I expect that the new ice-breaker will be built in Canada and will be a credit to the fleet belonging to the Government. My hon. friend can testify as to the ability of our shipbuilders. Last year we inspected the Bellechasse and the Dollard at Kingston. I believe these



two vessels are a credit to our Canadian shipbuilding firms. The same thing might be said of the other vessels that have been built at Sorel and in the Maritime provinces. I know that the iMontmagny is a splendid ship, very well equipped and of sufficiently large tonnage and draught. Really I do not see that for that class of ships we should not in the future give the preference to Canadian firms. At all events, we have now the declared policy of the hon. minister, and I must sincerely congratulate him on the decision which he has reached.

I agree entirely with what the hon. member for Rouville has said with regard to the building of ships in Canada with Canadian labour. I think that will please every member on this side of the House. I notice in the Auditor General's Report a statement that last year a ship called the Kestrel was sold for $5,000 to one Armstrong. What is the policy of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries in regard to these ships? Are they sold by public auction, tender, or otherwise?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The Kestrel, which was under the supervision of the Naval department, had been absolutely condemned by all the naval officials.
How old was she?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: She was a very old and useless vessel. Offers of purchase of the vessel were publicly invited, but none were received. We then received an offer of $2,500 for her, but my deputy, who looked into the matter, said that we ought to get $7,500. We held the vessel for a time at that price, but without avail, and, receiving an offer of $5,000, we decided that we had better sell at that. The money was paid, and I believe that the gentleman who bought the vessel has been regretting the purchase ever since.
How much did it cost in the first place?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I have not that information.
Examiners of masters and mates, $16,500.
Mr. La\V :	What salary does the
Examiner of Masters and Mates at Yarmouth receive?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The examiner there,
Captain Murphy, receives $300.

Captain Bradford Hilton conducts a school at Yarmouth; is he not

entitled to a salary the same as the officers at Quebec, Oollingwood, North Sydney and: Victoria?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I understand that he is not an official of the department, and that he conducts a private school and receives tuition fees from those whom he instructs.

Is that a reason why Captain Hilton should not be placed on the list with the gentlemen at Quebec, North Sydney and other cities where schools are conducted?
#We have always had a school in Yarmouth, and quite a number of masters and mates receive their education there. Mr. Murphy conducted one for a number of years until he was appointed examiner and of course he could not then continue the school. I know that Captain Hilton has applied to the department for appointment; he is a very-competent official, and, in view of the fact that he conducts a school similar to that conducted by the officials in the other cities, I think he is entitled to a salary.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It may be that the gentleman referred to by my hon. friend would prefer to continue his private school and receive tuition fees, as in that way he might make a larger salary than he would receive from the Government. I believe it has never been the policy of this Government te establish Government schools at centres where private schools are being conducted. Government schools are established only in. towns or cities where there are men who want instruction, and where there are noprivate schools.

At what places have
these schools been established by the Government?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
There are navigation
schools operating this year in Vancouver,. Oollingwood, North Sydney, Quebec, Yarmouth, Halifax and St. John. The instructor at Vancouver is Captain Eddie; at Oollingwood, Captain Coles; at Quebec, Captain Lachance; at North Sydney, Captain Sutherland; at Halifax, the Technical College; at St. John, Captain Cole.
How many masters and mates were passed last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
In the eastern division,
70 masters and 38 mates; in the inland waters division, 85 masters and 37 mates; and in the western division, 43 masters and 48 mates.
Does the minister distinguish between deep sea captains and coasting captains?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
This statement does not
distinguish.

Possibly you have no
deep sea captains applying.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not know, but I think there would be some.

Some deep sea captains
passed last year. What are the salaries paid to the examiners of masters and mates?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Captain J. E. Murphy,
Yarmouth, $300; Captain James Sutherland, North Sydney, $300; Captain Alexander Cameron, Charlottetown, $600. At Quebec the examiner of masters and mates, Captain Lachance, also conducts a school and has other work, and so gets a larger salary. Captain George C. Coles, Colling-wood, gets $200; Captain A. D. Grant, Edmonton, Alberta, $200; Captain M. Thordarson, West Selkirk, Manitoba, $200; Captain James Gaudin, Victoria, $200; Captain Geo. Hallett, Nelson, $200; and the chief examiner of masters and mates for the Atlantic division, Captain W. R. Lugar, of Halifax, $1,800. The chief examiner at Toronto, Captain H. W. King, gets $1,800, and the chief examiner for the Pacific coast, Captain Chas. Eddie, of Vancouver, $1,800.

I see that Captain Murphy, examiner at Yarmouth, gets only $300, and the examiner at Charlottetown gets $600. Captain Murphy is one of the best men for that position to be found in the Dominion of Canada, and $500 looks like a pretty small sum.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The reason is that Mr. Cameron looks after the entire province of Prince Edward Island and the northern coast of New Brunswick.
There is only one other examiner in Nova Scotia.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
There is one at Halifax,
one at Yarmouth and one at North Sydney.
If there is any way in which the minister could give Captain Murphy more salary, I wish he would do so, because he is a very efficient man for the position.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The salary seems to be
small, but they are all about on a par. I shall look into the matter.
Rewards for saving life, including life-saving stations, $125,400.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The big end of this item is connected with life-saving stations. In connection with the awards for saving life, the usual course is that some one in the neighbourhood writes the department calling attention to some act worthy of recognition. This goes to the gentleman at the head of the life-saving department, Commander Thompson, formerly an officer in the Royal navy, who makes a report, and if the report is satisfactory the minister gives directions that some recognition in the way of a telescope or watch or something should be presented. No such rewards are ever given to any one in the employ of the department.
Does Commander Thompson institute any inquiry as to the circumstances?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: There is a blank form asking a number of questions with regard to the matter which is furnished to any person to be filled in.

There is a case in my mind where some time ago a vessel was wrecked in the district of L'Ardoise in the county of Richmond. The schooner Bohemia from Newfoundland, laden with fish, was driven on a reef and the crew were rescued by some of the residents of the district, Thos. Clannon and his brothers. They succeeded in landing the crew from this vessel at great risk to their own lives, and I think it would be a case where they should receive some recognition for their bravery.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I shall instruct the department to send the hon. gentleman one of the forms to be filled in.

The minister will remember that on the 17th of January I wrote a letter earnestly recommending to his attention Captain Edgar McKinnon of SS. Westport and Captain Adelbert McKinnon of SS. John L. Cann who displayed great bravery and skill in rescuing the passengers and crew of the steamer CSbequid, lost on Trinity Ledge. I am sure that if the minister looks into the matter of the saving of these lives he cannot fail to realize that these two captains as well as their crews, deserve some recognition from the department and from the people of this country. The newspapers all over Canada as well as in Great Britain and the United States have given these two captains every credit for the bravery they have shown in the rescue of these men. The steamer Westport, which is very small, was the first to go out to this steamer and 62 of her

passengers and crew were taken off before [DOT]dark after they had been on the wreck for thirty-six hours, exposed to dangers untold ;and with the liability of being washed off any moment. They were rescued and landed at Yarmouth that night. The John L. Cann came right after the Westport and rescued all but the captain and ten of the crew who remained on board until the next morning, when they were taken off and conveyed to St. John. I would ask the minister to take these matters into account and trust that a suitable reward will be given to these men. I doubt if you will find in Nova Scotia two men more capable to effect such a rescue. They are thorough seo -going men, born cf sea-going families, occupying high positions as ship captains in Nova Scotia, where we produce some of the best and most heroic men in the world.
I commend the matter to the minister and trust that these men, as well as their crews will be given suitable recognition by the department.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
This is not the first time the hon. member for Yarmouth has called my attention to this matter. My attention was called to it also by the hon. member for Digby (Mr. Jameson). Both of these gentlemen wrote me letters. The hon. member for Digby had spoken to me a day or two before and then wrote me a letter which reached me on the same day as that of the hon. member. Both hon. gentlemen did what was proper and right in calling attention to the bravery of the captains and crews of both the Westport and the Cann.
On hearing from the hon. gentleman who communicated with me, we gave instructions to Captain Thompson to inquire immediately into the facts of the case and make a report. The matter is being considered by the Department and will be dealt with as promptly as possible. The awards are not in the nature of pecuniary recompense, but take the form of a watch, telescope or something of that kind- simply something to show the appreciation of the Government of the country for acts of bravery done in the discharge of duty. Perhaps they are the more highly valued by the recipients than a money gift would be.

This is a branch of the service from which politics should be excluded, but, unfortunately, in my province at all events, politics have been allowed to enter. Last session I put a question on the Order paper asking the

minister for the papers in connection with the dismissal of Norman McIntosh, captain of the life-saving station at Souris, and the minister told me he did not wish to make public the reason for dismissal for Mr. McIntosh's sake, I thought something very serious must be the matter. The minister told me I could peruse the papers in his office. I went there, and saw that the charge against Mr. McIntosh was that he drank whisky and sometimes indulged too freely. I was relieved to find that that was the only charge that could be brought against him, but though there may be some truth in that charge, the man who was appointed to succeed him is a greater offender still. McIntosh was a man who had received one of the awards we are speaking of, for bravery in saving life. He and another young man volunteered to go to the rescue of two men in imminent danger of being drowned on a very stormy night. With wonderful courage and skill, they eventually succeeded in rescuing the two who had taken refuge in the rigging of their ship. Mr. McIntosh also received the Carnegie medal for the same act of bravery, and yet that man was dismissed from the public service. I think it is my duty to ask the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to make the charge against McIntosh public, so that the people of this country will not think there is any serious stain upon his character. Surely the minister must have allowed political considerations, perhaps unintentionally, to influence him in this particular case. Another question I would like to ask is, why was John Ryan dismissed from the lifesaving station at Priest Pond, and Mr. Campbell appointed in his place.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I have not the papers here, but if my hon. friend will repeat his question at some other time, whether we are on an item that appertains to this matter or not, I will give him the information.
I would also like to know why the boathouse at Souris was moved during last summer. I would like all the particulars.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I will get the information.

Might I also suggest that the minister give us a list of the other life-saving officers who were dismissed during the past year. I made an inquiry last year, and from 19 life-saving stations on the coast, I found that 12 officers have been dismissed, and some of them without any investigation being held

at all. In my constituency there was a man who held one of these Government awards for conspicuous bravery in saving life. He had occupied his position for 34 years and was a splendid officer. He was dismissed without any investigation whatever, and, so far as I know, for political reasons. If all the life-saving officers belonging to the Liberal party have been turned out of office we would like to know it. I think it would be advisable for us to have a complete * list of all the dismissals.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: My deputy minister informs me that John Eyan, whom my hon. friend from Prince Edward Island (Mr. Hughes) referred to a moment ago, resigned his position voluntarily; he was not dismissed.
Will the minister furnish us with that list ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Yes.
Investigation into wrecks, $18,400.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That is the same as last year. It covers the travelling expenses of the Dominion Wreck Commissioner, the travelling expenses of the British Commissioner, the travelling expenses of all witnesses, the salary of British Columbia Wreck Commissioner, stenographers' fees, legal services, services of assessors, services of interpreters, reporting and typewriting, preliminary inquiries, printing and unforeseen incidentals, fees which may be granted to acting wreck commissioners. The latter is only a small amount.
Will my hon. friend explain to the House what action was taken in regard to the Lady of Gaspe accident which occurred on the Eiver St. Lawrence during the summer near Cap de la Madeleine?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The statement I have
here is of the casualties for last year, not for the current year. I will get the information for my hon. friend.

Later on. I happen to know the owners of the ship, Messrs. Bouchard Bros., of Quebec, who are highly respectable people and very good navigators. The report goes against them and I do not dispute it. I do not know the facts. I have not followed the case and my information is derived from what I have read in the papers. I know, as a matter of fact, that the owners
of the ship, who were found in default by the commissioner appointed by the department, complained, after the investigation, that they had had no chance to explain their case clearly. The reason given was that the commissioner does not speak French. I do not know personally if that statement is true or not. I simply take the allegation of one of the defendants in the case.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Had he nautical assessors associated with him?

I cannot say; possibly
he had.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I should think that in a
case of that sort there would be nautical assessors who would be familiar with the French language.

Possibly so. I am told that one of the grievances is that the case was not made clear because the' commissioner did not speak French. Possibly there were others present who did speak French. I do not question at all the decision arrived at by the commissioner. I simply call the attention of my hon. friend to that fact to ascertain whether in such a case it would not be possible to give ample protection to both parties. I am sure that my hon. friend is quite well disposed and that he will see that in future no such complaint is possible. I say again that I do not dispute the decision. I think the decision wfis right, but at the same time this is one of the grievances of the defendants.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I think that my hon. friend is absolutely right. Whether the decision is right or not, the court should be so conducted that there would not be any ground given for a grievance in regard to the finding of the court, and it seems to me that in cases of that sort, if the Wreck Commissioner is unable to speak the French language, he should take pains to have associated with him nautical assessors who can. I know from my own experience at the bar how very unsatisfactory it is when you have to get the evidence of witnesses translated by means of an interpreter. I will call the attention of the Wreck Commissioner to the fact and give instructions that in future in cases of that sort, where the parties or witnesses do not speak the English language he shall have nautical assessors associated with him who know the French language.
At six o'clock the House resumed, and then took recess.

The House resumed at eight o'clock.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
The House again in Committee of Supply, Mr. Blondin in the Chair.
Civil Government-Department of Indian Affairs, $147,487.50.

Some years ago, an hospital was opened at Caughnawaga, for the benefit of the Iroquois Indians. This hospital was established through the charity of a good lady, who noticing that for the last ten or fifteen years contagious disease was prevalent amongst the members of the tribe, and that they had not the means to pay for proper treatment, out of her beneficence and with her own means opened an hospital on the reservation. When my hon. friend (Mr. Oliver) was Minister of the Interior, I represented the matter to him and he gave an annual grant of, I think, $500 or $600 to help this good lady in her work. I may say that the hospital is equally available to Protestants and Catholics. I now appeal to the present Minister of the Interior to increase that grant to something like $2,000, after, of course, he makes careful inquiries to satisfy himself of the merits of this institution, and I think he will find that the money will be well spent.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. J. ROCHE (Supt. General of Indian Affairs):
speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The grant last year was, I think, $800, and I understand it is rather a small hospital. I will make inquiries from the officials and see if it is possible to increase the grant.
Probably $1,500 would be sufficient.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Do you know the name of the medical man who is in charge of the hospital?

I do not, but I know
that the institution is run on a purely humanitarian basis.
Why the increase m the vote for sundries, under the head of ' contingencies?'

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
It is due to the change in the method of paying the travelling expenses.
Civil Government-Department of Customs. $330,987.50.
Why is there an increase in this vote?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. D. REID (Minister of Customs):
speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: There is just $1,000 of an increase on the sundries. The amount voted last session was sufficient, but the commissioner added $1,000 in case it might be required.

There is a considerable
increase in the number of officials of the second division, subdivision B.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
There are only two promotions in the whole list, but twenty-two new officers are recommended by the commissioner for next year. He recommends the appointment of sixteen new clerks in second division, subdivision B, ten with salaries of $1,000 each, six with salaries of $800 each, one new clerk in the third division, subdivision B, at a salary of $500, two messengers and one packer in the lower grade with salaries of $500 each.
On account of the extra work in the department we had to put on some temporary clerks. They were all selected by the Civil Service Commission.

The Department of Customs is largely a routine department, and an increase of sixteen clerks in one division is quite substantial. Though the Customs receipts have been increasing until recently, they are now on the decrease.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: We had to put on temporary clerks last year to keep the work going. They will now be put on the permanent staff.	[DOT]
If the revenue is decreasing, you will not require their services this year.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: We expect the revenue to increase within the next few months.

Who recommended this
increase?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
The Commissioner of Customs, Mr. McDougald, has made a state-

ment for me showing what he thinks is necessary in so far as new employees are concerned. He has consulted the heads of the different branches, and they have come to the conclusion that they require these clerks. These clerks were put on temporarily last year, but we can not put them on temporarily this year and pay them from some other fund. We have to put them on the permanent list.

How many temporary
employees were put on?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
About this number off and
on. This is a department in which it is absolutely necessary to have a sufficient number of clerks to check the entries and to do the work necessary to protect the revenue. The bon. gentleman will understand that the entries have to be checked in case of mistakes made by the appraisers or collectors in rates of duty.
