It is a department in which it is better to have a [DOT]sufficient number of clerks than to have it undermanned. I am taking the advice of officials in wrhom I have great confidence.

I quite agree that every department should be fully manned in [DOT]order to do the work properly. At the same time this looks like a very large increase, seeing that the revenue is decreasing. With all due deference to the hon. minister, I am sure that the revenue will not increase in the next few months.

What the hon. minister has said about the necessity of having a sufficient staff is very true, but as Parliament is here for the purpose of receiving and criticising information, I draw attention to the fact that some of the ministers are asking for an increase in the number of temporary clerks, while other ministers are asking for an increase in the number of permanent clerks. It is impossible for the House to keep any satisfactory track of the increases or decreases in the service when there is that movement from the temporary staff to the permanent staff and for a temporary staff instead of a permanent staff. It would be better if it were definitely arranged that, instead of employing temporary clerks, we employ permanent ones. Let it be arranged that way, and not in some of the departments increase the permanent staff this year, increase the temporary staff next year, and *then increase the permanent staff by the number of temporary clerks.
Supposing these additional clerks are appointed and there is a shortage in some other department, is it the custom of the different departments to assist each other by lending clerks?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: I do not know what the other departments do, but in the Department of Customs we keep on only those that are required. If we have to take on temporary clerks and there is not sufficient work for them to do, we let them go immediately.

You never make any
exchange?	.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: No.
Were the men who were employed temporarily last year certified by the Civil Service Commission before they were employed?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: For the inside service temporary clerks must have a certificate; for the outside service they do not require a certificate.
Is this vote entirely for the inside service?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: Yes.
Will the hon. minister give us the names of those whom he employed temporarily during last summer?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: I promise to give them to the hon. member to-morrow.

The Minister of Customs did not, in my humble estimation, answer the question that both the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) and myself put to him the other day in connection with the steamboat Alert. I thank the minister for the following part of his reply:
If on the occasion in question the Alert was not interfering with her regular cruise, I personally do not see any reason why any one, even the member for South Cape Breton himself, should not go on hoard, and proceed to their destination should the vessel he going in that direction.
The hon. minister said that the coasts down there are not accessible by boat. I want to point out to him that there is no part of the county of Victoria that is not accessible by land or sea. A regular line of boats runs down there. What I want to ask the minister is this: for what purpose was the Alert crossing those waters at that particular time? The time seemed to

synchronize with the departure of the Conservative candidate in Victoria county, and the Conservative organizer for the province of Nova Scotia. I brought to the hon. gentleman's attention the fact that certain barrels were taken from the bonded warehouse in North Sydney and hauled to the steamer Alert by the driver or carter of a local wholesale liquor dealer. The hon. minister has not yet given me any answer as to what freight was carried by the Alert on her northward trip. I do not think that it is proper for any boat in the employ of this Government to be the carrier of the candidates or organizers of any political party. I am told-and this was practically the minister's answer to my question the other day-that the Liberal party sinned in that respect. If they did so, then I say that they were sinners, but that does not justify the [DOT]present Government or any other government which may come into power in this country in following the same course. I wish to put this question to the minister now: On what business was the boat Alert cruising in those northern waters at this particular time, and what freight did she take on board at North Sydney?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: I take it for granted that the hon. gentleman knows that the Alert is employed to prevent smuggling along the coast. She is engaged by the year, I think, and an officer in that district has charge of the service.

What is that
officer's name?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: I think his name is Angus Young, of North Sydney. The steamer goes to North Sydney occasionally and keeps running back and forward along the coast, following any instructions that may be given by those in charge or by the captain himself, if he supposes that any smuggling -is being carried on along the coast.
The hon. member for Cape Breton says they had a load of liquor on board.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
I think in my reply to the hon. gentleman I said that so far as I was personally concerned, or so far as any one in Ottawa connected with the department was concerned, we knew nothing about the matter, and gave no instructions in any shape or form. As to the freight, I will make inquiries and give the hon. gentleman the information that he wants. I do not suppose this boat could take on very much freight, but she might have taken on some such goods as the hon. gen-
[Mr. Carroll. 3
tleman has mentioned. The hon. gentleman comes from that part of the country and knows whether or not these statements are correct. As I said the other day, if any person in that vicinity wanted to go along the coast, and the steamer was going there, I do not think there could be any objection to his going on board. Of course in this case it happened to be the candidate and the organizer.
What kind of smuggling would the hon. minister expect to be going on along these northern shores in the month of January ?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: They bring liquor from St. Pierre and Miquelon.
At this time of year ?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: Certainly, at any time of the year.
I suppose the hon. minister does not know very much about that part of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: I admit that I do not know very much about it, as far as that part of the country is concerned, because I have never been there myself. I am only giving the information which I got from the official in charge of that service.
Did the minister ask of the officer in North Sydney whether liquor was put on board the steamer on that particular occasion ?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: I asked the officer to get me the information which was requested.
Did he get it for you ?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: I read the other day the [DOT]memorandum he sent me.
There was nothing in the memorandum about the barrels of liquor.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: I will get the information for the hon. gentleman; I do not wish t,o withold it.

Under the statutes of Nova Scotia it is an offence to carry intoxicating liquor from one port in the province of Nova Scotia to another. This matter was brought to my attention by a gentleman of North Sydney who is interested in preventing the sale of liquor in that port, and he asked me to bring the matter before the House. The matter stands this way. The officers and crew of the tug Alert-the owners of which draw, I understand, in the vicinity of 818,000 a year from the Government-a Government boat which was supposed to be engaged in

preventing the smuggling of liquor into the ports of eastern Nova Scotia, committed a breach of the Nova Scotia Prohibition Act by carrying intoxicating liquor from North Sydney to the northern ports of Victoria county. This is not hearsay; it is a specific charge, coming from a gentle* man in the town of North Sydney, and it is that charge which I wish the hon. minister to investigate.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: I shall certainly have it investigated.
Is the captain of the boat in the employ of your department, or are you simply charterers of the boat ?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: We are charterers of the boat; we pay, I think, about ?15,000 a year for the service.

Have the owners or
lessees a right to use that boat for other than Government purposes?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: No, she is supposed to be entirely in the -customs service.
If the hon. minister learns that this boat was taken down into Victoria county purely for the purpose of carrying liquor for use in this election, what will he do with the officers dn question?	-

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: I would not care to consider that supposition; if the hon. gentleman will wait until I get the information, I shall be glad to answer him.

The hon. minister
himself has no doubt as to the purpose of that trip?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: I have a great deal of doubt. As far as the carrying of liquor is concerned, if the captain or anybody on board had a knowledge of the matter I do not believe they would take it on board. I should not be surprised to learn that they carried groceries or something of the kind, and that the newspapers published reports that they carried liquor, r cannot believe that they would put liquors on board to take down the coast.

As one sits in the House and listens to the remarks of the hon. minister on this occasion, one is amused when he remembers the way in which the soul of the hon. gentleman was shocked a few years ago over some whisky that went up to the Arctic ocean. Hon. gentlemen from -Ontario who never cease talking about the operations of the
steamer Minnie M. might well transfer all *their vocabulary	and	a large part ofthe indignation which they have always /assumed with regard to that matter *to the performance of the Alert, which, no doubt, will became quite as famous in that	direction as	any of	the	celebrated	steamers	of	which	we	havepreviously heard so much. In attempting to	make	this	House	and	the
country believe that vessels come from St. Pierre and Miquelon in the middle of January and try to smuggle liquor to the shores of northern Cape Breton* the minister is drawing a very long bow. His commissioner comes from Nova Scotia, and if the minister does not know, the commissioner does know that access to the shores of Cape Breton by means of a schooner or sailing vessel at that season of the year is an absolute impossibility. As a matter of fact, there are no vessels trading between Newfoundland and Cape Breton and Nova Scotia and those northern waters at this season of the year. Consequently there was no necessity for the Alert to go up to the northern portion of Victoria county to look for smugglers, and everybody, including his friends from Nova Scotia, knows that that is so. Everybody knows that the facts* were that the Alert started off with the Conservative organizer and the Conservative candidate on a purely political mission. They were not looking for smugglers, they knew that there were none there and that none could get there, and they never expected to find any. The minister would like to jolly this thing along and amuse the House in regard to looking for information. Let me ask the minister if he has found out that the Conservative organizer of the province of Nova Scotia and the candidate for Victoria county were aboard that steamer.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: Yes, I gave the answer yesterday; it is in 'Hansard.'

The minister knows that. He has not found out whether there was any whiskey there or not, that is the only question about which he is in the dark. The minister does not need to wait till he gets information from North Sydney, he can find it in the department among his officials who know that the story about this boat going up to look for smugglers is grotesque and absurd. She started on this trip for one purpose, to take the Conservative candidate in the local election up to the northern part of Cape Breton. The only point at issue is whether

they took the supply of whiskey with them. The hon. member for Cape Breton has information from a reliable authority to the effect that they did, and when the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) wants to know what the minister is going to do if he finds that the whisky was there, it is a pertinent question. Does the minister think it improper for these men to have taken *any whisky there?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: Certainly.

So it appears that the Government are paying large sums to hire a steamer to carry electioneers in provincial elections around the province of -Nova Scotia. That is where the minister stands in regard to this question, and he -cannot get away from it. What does the minister proposes to do in regard to the utilizing of this boat for purely political .purposes? If the minister had one-half the good intentions that he pretended to have wnen he sat on this side of the House, he would at once cancel this contract, in order that the Government might he able to claim that at least they had carried out *one of their election pledges in regard to honesty of government.
Would the minister tell us what are the regular trips of the Alert? He tried to make the House infer that she *was going on some kind of a regular trip.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: I understand that the headquarters of the steamer are at North Sydney, and she cruises around looking for -smugglers.
What kind of smugglers do they expect to meet?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: I cannot say that, but I understand the steamer cruises around at whatever time she is likely to catch smugglers.

Why does not the minis-'ter despatch somebody from Ottawa to bring the boat back to North Sydney? Because I can assure him that if she has gone there with the organizer and candidate there is grave doubt of her ever coming back.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: Then, we will not have to pay Tor her hire.
Why should not the minister send somebody after her?

There is one addition
*to subdivision B of the first division in the minister's department.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
We are going to promote one clerk from the division below, and add another to that class.
Mr. MURPH1T: Who is to be promoted?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
The commissioner has not
given me any information, but it is some clerk who has been at the top of his class for some years.
On the item of contingencies, is the increase of .$1,000 due, as was explained in reference to other departments, to the new system of charging travelling expenses?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
The commissioner informs
me that this $1,000 will be required for travelling expenses.
Is the increase represented by that?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: Y"es.

This afternoon there
was a reference to a boat that had been brought to the Prescott shipyards. My hon. friend from Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) made some inquiry in regard to it, and the minister read a ..statement sent to him by the department. It is possible that the hon. member for Rouville was under a misapprehension about the boat having been purchased by the Customs Department, and I want to ask the minister if his department has anything to do with the shipyard at Prescott?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
The Customs Department
have nothing whatever to do with the shipyard at Prescott. I may add that the Customs Department knows nothing of any steamer having been purchased during the last fiscal year or up to date this year. There is a little yacht that was seized by the customs and not claimed. After it was repaired by the Marine Department the Customs Department paid the Marine Department for the work they did on this yacht. They immediately left the wharf at Prescott, went to Kingston, remained there a couple of days and went down the Rideau canal to St. John, N.B., where the boat is now in service. The only boats I know of that 'have ever been around Prescott, are the Scout and the Reserve. There was another large vessel there this winter belonging to the Marine Department and used in the surveying of the lakes. I do not know whether the department have bought a small launch for marine work at Prescott; if they have I have never seen it. I would not say that they have not a launeh of that

kind. It strikes me that I did hear something to that effect this summer. They were thinking of getting a gasolene launch for the superintendent to use in case the Scout and Reserve were away. But that is only what I heard.

The boat to which my
hon. friend the Minister of Customs has just referred to is different from the craft in regard to which my hon. friend from Rouville made inquiry, and in reference to which I offered some observations to the committee. This boat, I am informed, was brought to Prescott on October 26 last. She was not towed there as my hon. friend from Rouville said. I understand she went there under her own power. She stopped at Valleyfield on the way up, and one of the gentlemen in charge represented himself to be an official, I think he said the private secretary of my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works. I think he was drawing rather a long bow in making that statement, but that is how he described himself. The yacht bore no name, and reached Prescott on October 26, shortly after the Chateauguay election. Nobody knows the name of the yacht-it was taken off, and 1 understand she is still without a name. My further information is that she was purchased from the Shea Sales Company of Montreal. I am giving this information to my hon. friend so that he can make inquiry. We on this side will make further inquiry later on. A description of the boat may help my hon. friend. She is 35 feet long, four cylinder engine, with a speed of about 13 miles an hour, nickel-plated wind shield, auto-top, round stern, and hull painted white. These particulars may enable my hon. friend to identify her, and if it is not his department that is concerned with the purchase, I assume it must be the department of my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works or the Department of Marine and Fisheries. In any event, I am giving my hon. friend these particulars so that inquiries about this myterious craft may be made.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
I am very glad to get the
information. I may say it is all news to me. I never heard of this boat before and have never seen her and until the hon. gentleman just mentioned it, I never knew there was such a boat in existence. The boat is certainly not being used in connection with the Customs Department.
It must be in connection with the Marine and Fisheries or Public Works.

I would like to say a
word or two about a question I asked the hon. Minister of Customs this afternoon in regard to blank forms used by the customs being printed in both English and French. My hon. friend seems to be under the impression that this is being asked as a favour by the importers of Montreal. My hon. friend said this afternoon, are we going to print blank forms in German, for instance, for the benefit of German exporters? I called the attention of my hon. friend to the fact that all official documents relating to the Dominion Government, blue books, etc., are published in both languages. We do not ask the Government to go to the useless expense of having these forms printed in both languages in cities or towns where there are no French-speaking people, but my hon. friend will understand that in Montreal there is a large commercial community, some of them speaking English and some of them speaking French, and if the merchants ask for these blank forms to be printed in French as well as English-and you can have the both languages printed on the same form without duplicating the form itself-they are simply asking for what is their right, they are not seeking favours. I would like an answer from my hon. friend as to whether or not he will yield to the demand made by the Montreal importers, that these blank forms be printed in French as well as in English. My hon. friend will recall the illustration I gave him this afternoon of a Montreal importer sending one of these forms to an exporter in France who did not understand the English language. The form had to be sent back, and that took up a large amount of time. There is a general complaint about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
The form that the hon. gentleman handed me is simply the form of an invoice showing the kind of form the department approves of. The exporter in a foreign country makes out his own invoices and we accept them if they are in this form. The form I have here is not a customs entry form at all. We do not supply these forms to be sent away in large quantities. If a person were to go into the customs office with an entry form printed in French it is accepted, if it is made out in the right way, just as readily as a form printed in English. The misunderstanding between my hon. friend from Rouville and myself is over this form, and as I have said it is simply a form of invoice and not a

customs entry at all. We do not get these forms printed; they are printed by the firms themselves.

The answer of my hon. friend satisfies me. My correspondent informed me that he was handed a form by the customs authorities in Montreal which was printed in English. It was sent to France and sent back again because the exporter did not understand the English language. If my hon. friend will say that both languages can be used on these forms in Montreal or in any other place where both languages are spoken, I shall be perfectly satisfied.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
Certainly. If any person
comes into the custom house in Montreal or any place else with an entry form in French we will accept it.
And the blank form is supplied by the department?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: It is supplied by the department. This is headed ' Specimen form of invoice approved by the Canadian Customs.' This is in the-English language. If any person is sending to France, Germany, or any other place for goods he wants to have the proper form of invoice. Invoices come here without the necessary declaration and it makes a whole lot of trouble. These are a few specimen copies that they have in the department, and if a man comes and asks for the specimen we give him a form like this one.

They should be printed in French because they are supplied by the department for the information of the exporter. The difficulty was that the specimen in English was not understood by the exporter. I would ask the hon. gentleman if he intends in future to see that these blank forms are printed in both languages.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: Yes, I have no objection.

I am perfectly satisfied. The hon. gentleman seemed to be under the impression this afternoon that it was not a matter of right but a matter of favour. It is a matter of right. People dealing with the customs are entitled to have these forms in the French language when they are French-speaking people.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: There is ho doubt about that.

The Grand Trunk and
Canadian Pacific Railway Companies in the province of Quebec have all their forms, tickets and everything printed in both languages. It is a matter of convenience

and a matter of business. In all departments where they are doing business in the province of Quebec the same principle-should be applied.

Where is the Alert
now?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: I would be very glad to give the hon. gentleman the information if I could. I can hardly tell. She left North Sydney to cruise along the coast.
Not at all; she never went there to cruise for smugglers.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: That is my information.

The hon. gentleman has no such information, because everybody-in Cape Breton knows that at this season of the year it is ridiculous to talk about smugglers. To make the statement or to suggest the theory that the Alert, or any other Government steamer, would go along the north shore of Cape Breton to look for smugglers at this season of the year is to suggest something that is absurd. Perhaps the minister does not know that he is attempting to perpetrate a joke upon this House, but I may tell him that he is. I think the minister, in view of the fact that hon. gentlemen, when sitting on this side of the House, raised such a serious question in regard to the employment of steamers in connection with election work, is entitled to-give us the fullest information with regard to this matter before he can expect to get any supplies. My hon. friend should ascertain and let the committee know when the Alert went up there before. How many trips had she made since the middle of December in connection with preventive work in that part of the country? Would he tell us whether or not he is aware of the fact that there is a steamer running from North Sydney up as far as Neil's harbour on that coast subsidized by this Government, a public conveyance by which the Conservative electioneers and agents could have gone up there if they wanted to without appropriating a Government steamer which was put there for their own convenience in order that they could stop where-ever they wanted to, and could do so at the public expense? The minister is not going to get off with jollying the thing along and joking about smugglers in midwinter from St. Pierre and that kind of thing. This committee know how the hon. gentleman, in previous Parliaments, dealt with questions like this when they came up. My hon. friend ought not to attempt to abuse the intelligence of this House by perpetrating

such a theory upon them as that smuggling *was going on at this time of the year. My hon. friend's Government sent a special ice-breaker, the Stanley, up along the northern coast to go to the Magdalen Islands right through the waters in which this steamer is said to be cruising and the idea of smugglers coming over from St. Pierre in midwinter is one that is so grotesque that my hon. friend has a great deal of assurance if he fancies that he can get away with a story of that kind. In view of the facts in connection with this matter the minister h,as a Tight to supply the committee with full information as to what previous trips the Alert has made up that coast within the last two months for the purpose of stopping smugglers.
If a steamer could not carry on smuggling for the reason that she could not get into shore during the winter how could a steamer land political agents?

I did not say that
a steamer could not get into shore in winter time. I was speaking of the extent to. which vessels, at this season of the year, engage in that trade. Everyone knows very well that no vessels, except the Bruce which runs from Point au Basque to Sydney, and this steamer which runs from Sydney up along that coast, are navigating those waters in winter time. The navigation is such in the gulf of St. Lawrence-and this is in the gulf-that, with the exception of special steamers which have been running up this coast for the past few years, there is no trade of any kind going on in these months and the theory of smuggling is per fectly ridiculous.
That would be a good time for smugglers.

I am not familiar
with the time when they smug-9 p.m. gle up on lake Ontario, but that is not the time they smuggle in Nova Scotia. My hon. friend the Minister of Customs should bring down to this committee any report-and I venture to say he has none-from his preventive officer or anybody else suggesting there has been any smuggling along that coast since the middle of December. The minister cannot produce from any official of his department any suggestion, any report, stating that any smuggling has 'been carried on along these coasts since the 15th of December. My hon. friend intimated that his department was very generous. He said:
The member for South Cape Breton is aware that certain parts of the coast are inaccessible except by boat, and if on the occasion in question the Alert was not interfering- with her regular cruise, X, personally do not see any reason why any one, even the member for South Cape Breton himself, should not go on board, and proceed to their destination, should the vessel be going in that direction.
The facts in regard to this matter are these: It was not necessary for the public business for the Alert to go up along that coast. Instead of her going there to stop smuggling she went up there at the dictation of the Conservative managers in the county of Victoria who are running a provincial election for the purpose of taking the candidate and the organizer to different places in this constituency. She did not go up there to prevent smuggling and take these gentlemen along with her incidentally; she went there for that sole and specific purpose. The information which my hon. friend from South Cape Breton (Mr. Carroll) that she went there with a large supply of whiskey, to accompany these gentlemen, is of such ^ character that the minister ought to deal with it in the most serious way. Hon. gentlemen who have heard this same gentleman, who is now the Minister of Customs, inveigh in the strongest possible language against the employment of Government vessels for political purposes, sit in wonderment at the placid way in which he would like to jolly this question along. One of the great boasts of the Ministry was that when they came into power we were to have an ideal condition in regard to all questions of dealing with elections. They have been in for nearly three years and not only has nothing been done but here we have the Minnie M. outdone by the direct employment at the public expense of a Government vessel supposed to be engaged in the revenue service for the purpose of carrying organizers and whiskey to an outlying part of the province of Nova Scotia. I say to my hon. friend that before he asks this committee to vote supplies he should give to the committee all the reports there are from his officials that would show that this vessel had been employed in the month of January in preventive work along that coast and if he has not such reports he should tell the House so. In view of the statement of a member of this House, that whisky was placed on board the steamer in connection with these political organizers, an investigation should at once be held. The strong position taken on such matters, by the Minister of Customs in the

past, makes it impossible for him to escape instituting an investigation.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: The other day I gave the hon. member all the information I had up to that time.
You gave us no information that she went there to prevent smuggling.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: That is the service she is employed in.
You had no information to that effect then?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: All the officers tell me that is the service she is employed in.
Nobody told you she went up there for that purpose on this occasion?
Order.
Order what? Do these gentlemen not know that in committee a member can speak as often as he likes; the minister is not complaining.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: She cruises around the coast of Cape Breton for the purpose of preventing smuggling.

In the month of
January? Would the minister bring down any such statement in writing?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
I can obtain a report from
the officials, and when I get it I will have an investigation made. I can say that it was not on any instructions from Ottawa. If the officials at Sydney have taken upon themselves to carry these gentlemen to Neil's Harbour, I cannot help it now, but I will have an investigation made and I shall not permit one of the steamers of the department to be engaged in any such work. If the hon. gentleman does not wish to let the item go through then I will have to let it stand, or, we can hold one of these items over and I can bring down the information before it is passed.

I have no desire to obstruct the passage of any legitimate item. If the minister states to this committee that he will make inquiry into the facts as desired by hon. gentlemen on this side of the House, and that he will deal with these officials in accordance with the proper principles of government in such cases, I am satisfied. I rely upon the word of the minister to that effect. But I attach the condition that the investigation must be immediate.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: I will get all the information.
As speedily as possible?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: As speedily as possible.
If the minister finds several barrels of whisky on board will he order its confiscation?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: I should think it would be confiscated long ago.
He will not find any there now.

Is it necessary that this
vessel should clear from customs when going on these trips to round up smugglers?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
I should not think it would be necessary for a customs steamer to clear, for the reason that the captain is an acting preventive officer, and therefore there would always be a customs officer on board.
Mr. KYTE; Then there would be no entry in the customs office as to what cargo she carried?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: I do not think so, but if there is such a record I will bring it down with the report.

The minister will remember that last year I called his attention to the dismissal of the sub-collector of customs at Lameque (Shippegan), in my county. It took two investigations to discover some fault against this officer, who was a model civil servant; one of the best educated men in the county, and against whom no charge of partisanship could ever be justly made. After two investigations he was found guilty of having attended my meeting in September, 1911, and the worst charged against him was that he applauded some remarks of mine. I also pointed out to the minister that the man appointed in his place is a partisan every day of his life, and belongs to the party organization committee. The minister told me that if he ascertained that this official was guilty of partisanship he would have to stop it. Since then a municipal election took place in Gloucester county and the new appointee was the Conservative candidate, running his election on federal politics more than municipal issues. I have no fault to find with that if it is allowed to everybody. The minister in reply to a question yesterday stated that the sub-collector of customs at Lameque, as well as the sub-collector at Tracadie had not received per-

mission from him to be candidates in the municipal election, and I was pleased to have that statement. The municipal election to which I refer took place between the new appointee and the dismissed official, and some gentlemen present will be glad to hear that the dismissed official was elected by a vote of three to one against the Conservative appointee. All the same that does not carry out the pledge of the minister that if the present official was a partisan he would he dismissed. Some officials in my county have been dismissed on the sole recommendation of the defeated candidate, notwithstanding that they were no more active in politics during the fifteen years of Liberal rule than the Minister of Trade and Commerce stated publicly in the House an official might be. What will become now of this sub-collector of customs at Lameque who has been a candidate in municipal elections on a political platform, and who has been telling the people that he 'has the support of the federal Administration as well as of the Conservative Administration of New Brunswick. Will the minister take my word for it, as he has taken the word of the defeated candidate in other cases, and dismiss this man?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
I take the word of the hon. member without question, as to the subcollector taking part in a municipal election. As I understand it, the hon. member asks that I dismiss this man for taking part in the municipal election at Gloucester. As far as I am concerned, I feel that when a person accepts a Government position he should cease to take part in any election, municipal or otherwise. It seems, however, to have been recognized, both by the late Government and the one previous to that, that Government officials are allowed to take part in municipal elections. During the last municipal contest I had quite a number of complaints that civil servants who were Liberals had taken part, and their dismissal was requested. I have also had requests made by Liberals to be allowed to run for the mayoralty and other municipal offices. During the last year or two, in so far as the Department of Customs is concerned, there have been quite a number of officials running in municipal elections at different points. The same thing applies to all the other departments, the Department of Customs being no exception. I suppose the hon. member knows that in the city of Ottawa there
are Government officials holding quite important positions, such as city [DOT] councillors and controllers. At Kingston and other places the same thing occurs. Until there is a general rule that officials in all the departments shall cease to take part in municipal elections or to occupying positions on municipal councils, I am not in a position, so far as the Department of Customs is concerned, to refuse to allow them to do .so. During the last municipal election in January, only one official, a Liberal, asked me if I would have any objection to his-running. I explained to him that, as it had been allowed for so many years and as other civil servants were running, I could, not raise any objection in his case.
Did the man run?*

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: Yes, and he was elected.

I believe that in the city of Ottawa any gentleman in the Civil Service or outside of it must have had enough of the city's affairs to discuss without, mingling federal politics in his canvass. But when a candidate runs in a municipal1 election more on federal politics than on municipal issues, that alters the case. If I tell the hon. minister that this gentleman is still a member of the organization in his district, will he look into the matter?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: He must cease to be a member of the organization or else leave the service.
I am making the statement that he is still a member of the organization.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: I will make inquiries at once. He cannot hold the two positions.
I would also ask the hon. minister to inquire as to the subcollector at Tracadie.
What inquiry is the minister to make?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: Whether the gentleman is a member of the organization or not.
Is it against the rule for a Government employee to be a member of a political organization?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: Yes.
Is that the policy of the hon. minister or the policy of the Government?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: I can explain only in so far as my own department is concerned.

The hon. minister has again tonight laid down the policy of the Government as advanced last year by the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. White). When, during the absence of the hon. minister, I called the attention of the Government to dismissals in the Department of Customs in the county of Huntingdon, I stated that I had it on an authority which the minister himself would not dispute that in the first investigation the investigator reported that there was no cause for dismissal, but that the persistent demands of so-called independent candidates resulted in the minister chopping off the heads of two custom house officials in the county of Huntingdon, thus establishing a record that the county had not had since Confederation of dismissing men for political partisanship.
To-night we have had a good deal of information from our friends from the Maritime provinces in regard to the mission of a steamer along the coast, and apparently from their statements that vessel was called into the service to distribute liquor during the by-election. That seems to be the general policy of this Government. I want the minister to take note that we shall be prepared to prove in the courts that an official of this Government, appointed by this Government, working in an office close to that of the Minister of Customs in the city of Valleyfield, operated in the by-election in the county of Chateauguay and was caught red-handed distributing whisky on voting day right opposite the polling booth. I am not going to give the minister the name of that official. I make the bald statement. I want to know if the minister is going to investigate that case, and see that that man is no longer retained in the service of the Government. It may be offered in his defence that he was on holiday at that particular time. I want further to point out to the minister that one month later, in the provincial by-election in the county of Huntingdon, the same man was operating in the Conservative interest. All the pretensions of this Government will fall to pieces unless they are prepared to take up this case and to see that this particular man attends to his business as an official of the Government and keeps out of elections.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: Is he a customs official?

No, but his office is next door to the customs office in the same building right across the hall; and he was appointed by this Government, I think,

within a year. I submit that the Government has no reason to be proud of that record. Our friends claim that the election at Chateauguay was a victory for their naval policy and their trade policy. In view of the fact that their own candidate ran away from the naval policy, in view of the fact that our good friend the Postmaster General, speaking in Ormstown, in French, refused to discuss the naval policy, and in view of the evidence that we have that an official of this Government was distributing whisky on election day, it seems to me that the Government will have to revise their ideas on the result of that election. I hope the hon. minister will bring this to the attention of his leader and see to it that the Government officials in Valleyfield take no further part in elections.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
In referring to this
distribution of liquor, is the hon. gentleman speaking from personal knowledge or from hearsay?

I am speaking upon the
evidence of a man who was sent out there with two witnesses, and who caught the man in the act.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: Hearsay.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
Am I to understand
that the hon. gentleman said that I never
discussed the naval policy in Chateauguay?	,

I say that I sat in the hall and listened to the hon. minister's eloquent speech at Ormstown. Speaking in English, he made a casual reference to the naval policy, and speaking in French he never mentioned it in any way whatever.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: My hon. friend must have been asleep. I had been told by the people that when the right hon. leader of the Opposition, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) and the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) were in Ormstown on the previous day, they had avoided the discussion of their own naval policy. I was asked by the gentlemen who came to see me before the meeting if I would discuss both policies, and I did so. I told the people that the gentlemen who were in Ormstown the day before, apart from some abuse that they had heaped upon us, had avoided discussing their own policy. I said, you know all about our naval policy.
What is it?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: The matter was discussed here for months last session, and I take it that the electors of Chateauguay are intelligent enough to have heard something about it. I do not think there is a man in this country who does not know what our policy was last session.

What is it now?
What is your permanent policy?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: Our permanent policy does not exist. The Prime Minister has told my hon. friend that whenever there is a naval policy it will be put before the House and the people will be consulted about it. So, when the hon. member tells the House and the country that we did not discuss the naval policy on that occasion he is entirely wrong. I told the people what the Bill presented to Parliament last session was, and I said: We are going to discuss the naval policy as formulated by [DOT]the right hon. the leader of the Opposition. So the people heard what they had not been told on the previous day, and the result was that on election day we had a majority of seventy-five in Ormstown.
Allow me to correct the hon. Postmaster General. In Ormstown, where he spoke, there was a Liberal majority at the last by-election, whereas in 1911 there was a Conservative majority.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
My hon. friend does
not even know the result of the polling in Ormstown; I was sure he had been asleep. As a matter of fact, in 1911, there was a majority of twenty-six against us in Ormstown, and at the by-eleotion there was a majority of seventy-five in our favour.
The minister is talking about the parish. I repeat that in the village of Ormstown there v as a Liberal majority.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
I was not speaking
only of the village; I was speaking of the whole place.

Last year while the
Estimates for the Customs Department were before the House, I brought to the attention of the minister a grievance which some businessmen of Whitney Pier, which is a part of the city of Sydney, had in respect of the sub-collector of customs at that point, Mr. McDonald. They brought to my attention the fact that he is a merchant and an importer of goods, and that he carries on business in three different stores in the city. They instructed me to ask the minister whether or not it was within the knowledge of the hon. gentleman or of 28
his department that this gentleman was an importer of goods. I do not make any charge against this gentleman; I am only placing before the minister the complaint of the merchants to whom I have referred, that his being an importer of goods might cause him to have some advantage over them. At the time I brought the matter to the attention of the minister, he promised me that he would let the House know whether it would be the policy of the Government to allow importers of goods to act as customs collectors or sub-collectors. The House rose shortly after that, and I presume the minister did not have time to bring down the information. If he has not the information now, I hope he will get it and bring it down before his Estimates are all put through.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
It certainly is against the
rules of the department for any one occupying any such position to act as collector of customs. Obviously he would have an advantage over the other merchants, as he would see their invoices, the prices of their goods, and so on. When the hon. member brought the matter to my attention, I certainly must have referred it to the officials of the department, and no doubt there is a report on file. I will look into the matter to-morrow, and if this official is still engaged in the business to which my hon. friend refers he certainly must give up either his business or the position. Of course in some smaller places where the revenue is not very great, the salary of the official is so very small that there would be no objection to a farmer, for instance, acting as collector, but a merchant is certainly objectionable, and I cannot understand how the official can be continuing in that business and holding his office at the *same time. I shall look up the report on the matter and the hon. member will get it without fail.

I would like to have it
(Stated clearly whether or not officials of the Department of Customs are free to be candidates in municipal elections, and to take an active part in municipal life?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: This has been allowed in all the other departments. The matter was brought to my attention this year by one of our inspectors, who asked me if I had any objection to his taking part in municipal elections. I suppose it was really a political election too. I think his opponent was likely on the opposition side of polities. It was going on all over the country.
No order has been issued?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: No, and I have had complaints that certain Liberal customs officers took part in municipal elections and people have 'wanted them dismissed. On the other hand, the hon. member for Gloucester gives me an instance the other way, and I think there should be some rule. At the same time there is no general rule.

Some years ago a rule was issued by the Customs Department forbidding persons in the customs outside service to become candidates in municipal elections. In the province of Nova Scotia, in many instances, to my own knowledge, persons desirous of becoming municipal candidates who were in the customs service were prevented from running by the Minister of Customs. This rule may not have been observed in all cases, but I know of my own knowledge that customs officers contemplating entering municipal elections received word from the Minister of Customs that they could only do so on penalty of losing their offices. Further, in September and October of last year, the customs service was circularized by the Department at Ottawa in the same direction and persons in the service were told that they must not be candidates in municipal elections. I know that an order was made five or six years ago in connection with this matter. I think the minister is mistaken in saying that his department permitted anybody to take part in municipal elections as they saw fit. I think it is a rule that has been pretty generally observed in the past by the Customs Department.
Does the hon. member say that the previous Government forbade officers being candidates for municipal elections?

I say that an order to that effect was issued by the Customs Department, and in Nova Scotia it was fairly well observed. Of my own knowledge I know of two persons who were told that they should not be candidates in municipal contests.

It was not observed in Ontario. If that order was made to apply to Nova Scotia I would assume it would apply to the other provinces, and I can assure my hon. friend it did not apply in Ontario. A very estimable gentleman was a candidate for several years in Kingston, a very high customs official in that city and an adherent of the Liberal party, but a man who as customs officer took no part

in politics. This year, following the natural course of events, he ran in Kingston for mayor. There could not have been any general rule to prohibit customs officers [DOT]taking part in municipal elections. If there was in Ontario it was honoured more in the breach than in the observance.

Referring again to the
Chateauguay elections, from a report I have here, taken from the Montreal Gazette, giving the result of the polls in the village of Ormstown, where the minister spoke, poll No. 11, I see that Morris had 79 votes and Fisher 95, a majority of 16 for Fisher, and the large majorities in the parish of Ormstown were in those particular polls where the Government official had been operating.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: What is the use of splitting hairs? Ormstown comprises the township of Ormstown and the village of Ormstown. If you take those two places combined-and we had in our audience people not only from the small village but people from all over the township, the member knows that well, as the hall was crowded-and the people who voted the following day were not only the people of the village but of the whole township. If my hon. friend, who seems to have lost his memory as to what took place on that day, will refer not only to the village but to the whole township of Ormstown he will see that what I represented is true, that the majority of the Conservative candidate was 75.

The hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean), I have no doubt,, was trusting to his memory in making his observation that under the previous Administration the Minister of Customs laid down the law that customs officers should not participate in municipal elections.
Not at all; I know it as a fact.

I have a very distinct,
recollection of discussing the question with the late Minister of Customs four or five sessions ago for at least an hour, when I gave him specific instances where some collectors of customs were candidates for positions as councillors in elections run on straight party lines. Not only was I unable to get redress in cases of partisanship, but I was unable to get the late Minister of Customs to lay down the law that officials should not be permitted to run. What L believe is that collectors of customs in receipt of a fairly good salary ought not ta

be permitted to take part in municipal contests which are conducted along party lines and I think the sooner we come to an understanding in this country so that we will have one general policy for all Administrations the better. We will thus save this recrimination and bickering back and forth about petty officials and positions.
Will the minister inquire if his department did not, within six months, circularize the outside service against participation in municipal elections?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: I shall certainly do so, I have no recollections of the circular.

I have here ' Hansard '
of the session of 1910-11, at page 1055, of which the hon. member will find a full statement covering several pages, setting forth the position I took at the time.

I know and have personal knowledge of two cases at least where objections were made by electors of a municipal district against a certain person being a candidate who was in the customs service, occupying, of course, some minor position; and by reason of these protests he was requested by the Minister of Customs to withdraw from the contest.

By what Government
was he appointed?
By the late Government.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
What surprises me, if that
circular was sent out, is that it must have been sent to all officials and yet within the last few months many officials have taken part in these municipal contests and quite a number of them are not in sympathy with the Government. I have had complaints about customs employees appointed by my predecessor taking part in a municipal contest at Yarmouth, I think it was.

Perhaps it was
Annapolis county.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. member for Yarmouth would know if any such officials in Yarmouth took part in the municipal elections?
None whatever.

The junior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) has referred to Annapolis county. I may say in regard to that, that under the late Government there was a sub-collector of customs by the name of Mr. Porter who was a councillor and 28J
who ran in the Liberal interests. I wrote to the then Minister of Customs and asked him if it were not against the rules of his department to allow one of his officers to act on a municipal council, and I was given the reply that there was no such rule. As a matter of fact Mr. Porter sat in the municipal council for a great many years.

That was not the gentleman I had in mind at all when I interrupted. The minister was asked if a request had not been made for the removal of an official of his department for taking part in some municipal election. I do not claim that it is objectionable for an official to take part in a municipal election. I am more interested in the proposition that customs officials should not be candidates. I was told that one officer of the customs at Bridgetown, by the name of Mr. Hicks, was dismissed from office in December or January, 1913, because his son had taken part in a municipal election.

My hon. friend is misinformed in regard to that. No official in Annapolis county was dismissed on any such grounds as that. The firm to which this collector of customs belongs had tried to cajole voters at that municipal election, but that was not the cause for which the official was removed.

I think some good purpose is being served by this discussion. If is perhaps an opportune time to ask the Minister of Customs to lay down some rule which could be observed universally throughout the country. The observations made by the junior member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean), are absolutely correct and within my own knowledge, although possibly the circular sent out by the late Minister of Customs might not be described as ' instructions ' to customs officers not to take part in municipal politics. I am aware, however, tlat recommendations to that effect were issued to the warden of the county which I represent. He is a most competent official and highly qualified to discharge the duties of warden of the county. Six years ago I remember he was again asked to stand for his district in the municipal council, and he wrote to the Minister of Customs asking if any objection would be raised to him occupying a position on the municipal council, and as a result of the reply received by him from the late Minister of Customs, that gentleman did not offer as

a candidate and has not since been a candidate in the county of Richmond. Whether that rule is universal or not I am not aware, but I say that the late minister recommended that it would be better for that gentleman to take no part in municipal politics.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: So far as I aim concerned, I believe that every customs official should cease to take part in municipal elections or any other elections. I think, however, that if customs officials are prevented, the rule should be universal throughout the whole Service; it should apply to all departments. So far as I am concerned, I have not changed any rule that was in existence when I came into office in this regard. I am satisfied that if the records of the recent municipal elections throughout the Dominion were looked up, we should probably find as many officials of one political faith as of the other, who were candidates in the municipal elections. Of course there are places where it might be necessary for an official to take part in the election, say, in some new town. I remember receiving a letter about a year ago from an official in a new town asking me whether he could take office in the council, and I advised him that at the expiration of lids term of office it would be better for him to keep out of municipal contests altogether. I think that is what should be done and hope that some rule of that kind will be put into force throughout the whole service.

I have a very distinct
recollection of two cases during the last fifteen years, where an official was refused the right to take part in municipal elections. One was a case that occurred in Fredericton, concerning an inspector of fisheries, who wished to be a candidate for mayor. He was denied that right. That brings up the general question. My hon. friend the Minister of Justice has stated that in his judgment every official should be debarred the right to take part in municipal elections. I cannot agree with that, although perhaps in saying so I may not be in accord with the opinions of hon. gentlemen on this side. It seems to me that a rule should be laid down providing that the man who earns his living as an official, the man who receives sufficient salary on which to live, should be a public official and mind his own business. But the man who gets only a small amount of money, such as a poor preventive officer or a man in charge of a country post office

getting $35 a year, these are the men who should not be deprived of the right of citizenship. These men should be allowed to exercise their right and they should not lose their jobs when a new Government comes in, because, they have exercised their right of citizenship. But as I said before, in the case of a man earning his whole living in the public service, an entirely different principal should prevail, and I think it would be well for the Government to lay down some rule which would be fair and reasonable to compel Government officials to be Government officials and to allow the other men to be men amongst men and exercise the right which everybody supposes them to have.

I want to prefer a
very serious charge against the Minister of Customs, a charge that may bring about his removal from the Government. The charge is this:	he has been spreading a
very strong free trade sentiment in my constituency. I do not object to that, but I know his friends in my constituency do. A special officer was .sent to the customs port at Coutts during the past year. He was very active, and some of his offences were so serious that Conservatives were repeatedly going over to the Liberal ranks. I will instance a few cases, and in bringing this matter to the attention of the minister I may say that I am very anxious that he should keep this officer on the move throughout the whole country, because his operations will be of great assistance to the Liberal party. In one case a man drove across the boundary from Coutt's to Sweet-grass, Montana, and had luncheon at Sweet-grass because there did not happen to be an hotel at Coutts. He had a sheep camp at the boundary and while he was over he bought a pound of butter. When he came back his entire outfit, team of horses, wagon and pound of butter were seized and he had to go to Lethbridge and get another outfit. He had to put up the value of the team of horses and wagon, and the matter was in the hands of the Department of Customs for some time. There was another case far more serious than that. A gentleman living on the Canadian side of the line crossed to Sweetgrass, got a package of tobacco and when he came over the line the package of tobacco was seized. Innumerable cases of this kind have done a great deal to help free trade sentiment, and I only hope that the Minister of Customs will keep this man going about the country, not so much in the West, because

the sentiment is very strong there at the present time, but through the East. His name is Hughes and that is a name that is very helpful to the Liberal party.

I wish to bring to the
attention of the hon. Minister of Customs the matter of a return for which I asked last year. It was in connection with the dismissal of the collector of customs at the port of Glace Bay-Mr. M. J. McKinnon. There were two investigations into the charges that were preferred against Mr. McKinnon, and I was instructed by Mr. Duche-min on the occasion of the second investigation that his report, including the evidence taken in the first investigation, had been sent to the department. I got the documents in relation to the second investigation, and I brought to the attention of the minister, here in the corridors last spring, the fact that the return of papers I had asked for was not complete in that it did not contain the report of the first investigation into the charges of political partisanship. I wish to ask the minister if he will kindly bring down to the House the report of the first investigation including the evidence taken by the commissioner. I may tell him that I reqfiire this as I intend to discuss some phases of this dismissal when the Estimates for the outside service are brought down.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
Is the hon. gentleman sure
I did not bring that down? I brought down some reports the other day.
I got part of it last winter.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: I know I brought down some the other day and I thought that was included in the return. I shall bring down that report to-morrow.

While on this matter I desire to call the attention of the Minister of Customs to the case of the dismissal of Martin Johnston, preventive officer at Red Islands. This dismissal took place shortly after the present Government came into office and the reason given by the minister for the dismissal was that there was nothing for this officer to do and that his services were on that account dispensed with. But I was able to remind the minister that a few weeks afterwards they appointed another preventive officer to take his place.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: At the same point?

Oh, yes, practically the
same point. I desired to know
10 p.m. what the salary of the new preventive officer was, which information has not been given to me, and I would be glad if the minister would get the information. Michael E. Gilles of Irish Cove was appointed in his place, and I want to know what the salary of Mr. Gilles is and what salary Mr. Johnston enjoyed while he was in office.
Customs-Salaries and contingent expenses of the several ports in the Dominion, including pay for over-time officers, notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act, $3,590,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
I will explain this item.
The vote for the fiscal year 1913-14 was $3,290,000, and we are asking for $300,000 more this year. The total salaries of the officers employed at the various ports of the Dominion were, when the estimate was prepared, $2,760,445. The contingent expenses for the nine months ended 31st December, 1913, amounted to $337,845, and it is estimated that for the whole fiscal year we will require $394,745. Add to this the net over-time as expended during the year 1912-13 amounting to $124,000. That is to remunerate landing waiters and officers who work evertime at the different ports. That makes a total estimated expenditure of $3,279,190. From this total we deduct the estimated bonded warehouse refunds, based on those of the previous year, amounting to $32,000, bringing the estimated expenditure to $3,247,190. We ask for $3,590,000, there being an increase of $342,810 over the estimate of last year.
I suppose the largest increase is in the port of Montreal?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: Yes.

Would the hon. gentleman be kind enough to inform the House as to the number of customs officers that he found when he assumed office, and the increase in the numbers and salaries in the first, second and present years?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
I will make a note of that
so that I will be able to give the hon. gentleman the information. I could not give it offhand. I will get it for him before we pass these Estimates.

Would the minister at
thfe same time give us the total number of officers that he has appointed and dismissed in the whole Dominion of Canada since he assumed office?

Inasmuch as the Minister of Customs has, I think, only these items on page 96 to pass, I think he should not press for a vote to-night, but that we should take them up some other evening, because we have not had an opportunity of looking into them.

I would like to get the names and the increases in salaries for the port of Quebec for the same years when we take up these Estimates again.
Civil Government-Department of Railways and Canals, $201,150.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: The Minister of Kail-ways cannot be here to-night, as he is not permitted to come out after dinner, and I would ask hon. gentlemen to pass these items. One assistant engineer is dropped in A1 and an assistant engineer is appointed to Bl. In B2 there are two additional clerkships of $1,200 each, and in A3 five new clerks at salaries ranging from $500 to $1,200 per annum.
None of these are in the Moncton office?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: No.
Is the salary of Mr. Gutelius included in this?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: No.

I would like the
minister to bring down at as early a date as possible the Order in Council appointing Mr. Gutelius. The friends of the Government in the Maritime provinces are told when they ask something from the minister: Mr. Gutelius says it cannot be done. We would like to know whether Mr. Gutelius is bigger than the minister and just what his duties are.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
The Order in Council will be
brought down.

I would like also to have all the papers brought down in connection with the purchase of American coal by the Department of Railways in the month of December last. To-day the coal miners of Nova Scotia are lacking work, and it is rather unsatisfactory to know that the Government railway purchased coal in Pennsylvania, brought it by rail to Massena Springs, took it from Massena Springs to Levis and paid the freight on it to that point; while at the same time it declined the opportunity to haul coal over its own railway from the mines along the Intercolonial railway. There are quite a number of small mines, particularly, which are to-
,
day stopping for want of orders, and a great many others are working half time.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: The papers will be brought down and they will give all the information. I think I am right in stating that the coal companies informed Mr. Gutelius that they could not supply coal at the time it was wanted.

That is true with regard to two of the largest coal companies. The trouble is that the Government did not pursue their inquiries among a large number of other companies which could have supplied the coal. As a matter of fact, in the month of January when they purchased that coal, they proceeded to stop the delivery of coal by the larger companies in the province. To say that, all of a sudden, the Intercolonial railway should demand 1,500 tons of coal, to the exclusion of other purchasers, is not fair, when all they had to do was to wait their turn and they could get the coal and haul it over their own railway. I want all the information brought down at once, because I intend to discuss the subject very fully later on.
Apparently the department, according to the detailed statement in the Estimates, is going to employ five additional solicitors, at salaries ranging from $1,000 down.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: There is only one department solicitor.

If that is so the item is very badly worded, because any person reading it would take it to mean that there were to be five departmental solicitors appointed. Who is the departmental solicitor for whom a salary of $4,000 is provided?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: No one has been selected for that position up to the present time.
What is Mr. Aylward's position in the department?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: He was departmental solicitor, but he is down at Moncton now, and not in the department. This is to fill the position formerly occupied by him.
Then there would appear to be a number of right-of-way agents, with salaries ranging from $3,600 down. Are all these officials to be added to the staff of the department here?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
No; that represents the number of officials in that subdivision. There

were fourteen in the subdivision last year and this year there is one less. The right oi way and lease agent is Mr. R. H. Fraser. The other officials are men who have been there for years, and have been advanced to these positions.
Has Mr. Fraser been appointed recently?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: He was appointed some time ago.
Where is he from?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: He is from Nova Scotia, I think.
Does he come from my county?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: I think so.

[DOT] Does the hon. minister know the position that Mr. C. Campbell holds at
*the present time?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: I can give the names of the fourteen officials. The position of departmental solicitor is vacant. L. K. Jones, Assistant Deputy Minister; E. V. Johnson, inspecting engineer; John Murphy, electrical engineer; J. L. Payne, comptroller of statistics; R. H. Fraser, right of way and lease agent; G. A. Bell, financial comptroller; L. Sherwood, principal assistant and designing engineer; W. C. Little, accountant and superintendent of stationery; F. A. Dixon, chief of correspondence; G. A. Mothersill, auditing engineer; W. V. Cope, departmental auditor. There is one position vacant, that of assistant engineer. Last year %ve had another assistant engineer, but that position has been dropped this year. Mr. C. Campbell would not be on the list, a3 this is only for employees in the building.
You have made five additions to the third division, subdivision A. What are they for?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: Those positions have not been filled. They are clerkships at $900 each.
Under the Civil Service Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: Yes, they will be appointed by the commission.
Will they be employed in the department here?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: Yes.

Will the minister
tell us anything about extending the Civil Service rules to that branch of the Department of Railways and Canals at Moncton?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: I cannot give the hon. gentleman any information about that. I went into these Estimates with the officials, in order to understand them thoroughly so far as the inside service at Ottawa is concerned, and nothing further.

A statement has
been made in the'press in the province of Nova Scotia that the department contemplate the construction of a diversion of the railway in the eastern part of the province, and that there is to be a new part of the railway constructed along the north shore of Nova Scotia east of New Glasgow. I would like the minister to bring down what correspondence there has been with Mr. R. P. Fraser of Pictou with regard to that diversion of the line.
